subtopics.title: Amplifiers
subtopics.subtitle: What amplifiers do, how they are classified, and what the NEC exam asks about them

concepts.text: What an Amplifier Does

An amplifier is an electronic circuit that increases the amplitude of a signal (its voltage, current or power) while preserving its waveform. The extra output power is not created from the signal: an active device (BJT, MOSFET or op-amp) uses the small input signal to control how much power is drawn from the DC supply and delivered to the load. The ratio of output to input is the gain, and an amplifier is judged by its gain, bandwidth, input and output impedance, distortion and efficiency.
Roadmap of This Topic
The four subtopics that follow build on each other:
items: Amplifier Basics: gain and decibels, impedances, bandwidth, distortion, efficiency, coupling and cascading.
Classification of Output Stages: where the Q-point sits on the load line and the resulting classes A, B, AB, C and D.
Comparison of Amplifier Classes: efficiency derivations (25 %, 50 %, 78.5 %), distortion, heat, cost and applications.
Biasing Class AB Output Stage: removing crossover distortion with diode or V_BE-multiplier bias while keeping efficiency high.

concepts.text: How Amplifiers Are Classified
The same amplifier can be named in several ways, depending on the property being described:
items: By signal size: small-signal (voltage) amplifiers handle millivolt inputs in the linear region; large-signal (power) amplifiers drive loads such as loudspeakers and antennas, where efficiency and distortion matter most.
By frequency range: audio (20 Hz to 20 kHz), radio-frequency (tuned, narrow band), video or wideband (a few hertz to several megahertz) and DC amplifiers (respond down to 0 Hz).
By inter-stage coupling: RC (capacitor) coupled, transformer coupled or direct coupled.

By conduction angle, the part of the input cycle during which the output device carries current: class A (360°), class B (180°), class AB (between 180° and 360°), class C (less than 180°), and class D, in which the devices switch fully on and off.
By configuration of the active device: common-emitter, common-base and common-collector (emitter follower) for BJTs, or common-source, common-gate and common-drain for FETs.

rows: Lowest distortion; small-signal stages, hi-fi where heat is acceptable
Crossover distortion at zero crossing; push-pull power stages
Very low distortion with a small bias; most audio power amplifiers
Heavily distorted pulses restored by a tuned load; RF transmitters, frequency multipliers
Low distortion after LC filtering; portable and battery-powered audio

concepts.text: Key terms you must be able to define:
items: Gain: ratio of output to input quantity; in decibels, 20 log for voltage or current and 10 log for power.
Bandwidth: frequency range between the lower and upper cut-off frequencies, where gain stays within 3 dB (70.7 %) of its mid-band value.
Q-point (quiescent point): the DC operating point (I_CQ, V_CEQ) fixed by the bias network with no signal applied.
Load line: the straight line of possible (V_CE, I_C) pairs for a given supply and load; the signal moves the operating point along it.
Conduction angle: the number of degrees of each 360° input cycle during which the output transistor conducts.
Efficiency: AC signal power delivered to the load divided by DC power drawn from the supply.
Crossover distortion: the notch produced near zero output when neither transistor of a class B pair is conducting.
Push-pull: two devices driven in antiphase so that each handles one half-cycle; even harmonics cancel.

concepts.text: How the Exam Tests This Area

Exam MCQs on amplifiers are mostly one-line recall items: matching a conduction angle to a class, quoting the maximum efficiency of class A (25 % or 50 %) and class B (78.5 %), naming the class that suffers crossover distortion (B) and the one that cures it (AB), identifying the class used for audio power (AB) or for RF tuned stages (C), and describing class D as a switching amplifier. Numerical items convert gains to decibels or compute efficiency from P_ac and P_dc, so keep the dB rules and the efficiency numbers at your fingertips.
Going Deeper: Amplifier Models and Feedback

Any linear amplifier can be drawn as a two-port with an input resistance R_i, an output resistance R_o and a controlled source. Which source is used depends on the input and output quantities: a voltage amplifier has a voltage-controlled voltage source A_vo·v_i, a current amplifier a current-controlled current source A_is·i_i, a transconductance amplifier a voltage-controlled current source G_m·v_i, and a transresistance amplifier a current-controlled voltage source R_m·i_i. The four models are interchangeable for a given circuit (for example G_m = A_vo/R_o), but the one whose ideal impedances match the real circuit gives the simplest analysis.

With a real source and load, each port forms a voltage divider, so the gain actually obtained is smaller than the open-circuit gain. For a voltage amplifier fed from a source of resistance R_s and driving R_L, only R_i/(R_i + R_s) of the source voltage reaches the input and only R_L/(R_L + R_o) of the internal voltage reaches the load. In a cascade the next stage's R_i is the load of the previous one, so every interface costs a divider factor; this is why buffers (high R_i, low R_o) are placed between stages.

concepts.plainText: vo/vs = [Ri/(Ri + Rs)] · Avo · [RL/(RL + Ro)]

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: loaded voltage amplifier
v_s = 10 mV, R_s = 10 kΩ, R_i = 40 kΩ, A_vo = 100, R_o = 1 kΩ, R_L = 4 kΩ
v_i = 10 mV × 40/(40 + 10) = 8 mV
v_o = 100 × 8 mV × 4/(4 + 1) = 0.64 V
A_v = v_o/v_i = 80;  overall v_o/v_s = 64 = 20 log 64 = 36.1 dB
P_i = v_i²/R_i = (8 mV)²/40 kΩ = 1.6 nW
P_o = v_o²/R_L = (0.64 V)²/4 kΩ = 102.4 µW
A_p = 64 000 = 10 log 64 000 = 48.1 dB  (not 20 log 80, since R_i ≠ R_L)

Negative feedback returns a fraction β of the output and subtracts it from the input. If A is the gain without feedback, the closed-loop gain is A_f = A/(1 + Aβ); the quantity 1 + Aβ is the amount of feedback (desensitivity), often quoted in dB as 20 log(1 + Aβ). When Aβ >> 1 the gain approaches 1/β and depends only on the passive feedback network. The same factor that divides the gain also divides fractional gain changes, harmonic distortion and noise generated inside the loop, widens the bandwidth (f_H rises and f_L falls by 1 + Aβ, so the gain-bandwidth product stays constant) and multiplies or divides the input and output resistances. Positive feedback (Aβ subtracting from 1) raises the gain and is used deliberately only in oscillators and Schmitt triggers.

concepts.latex: A_f = \frac{A}{1 + A\beta},\quad \frac{dA_f}{A_f} = \frac{1}{1 + A\beta}\,\frac{dA}{A},\quad f_{Hf} = f_H(1 + A\beta)
concepts.plainText: Af = A/(1 + Aβ); dAf/Af = (dA/A)/(1 + Aβ); fHf = fH(1 + Aβ), fLf = fL/(1 + Aβ)

concepts.text:
Worked example 2: voltage-series feedback
A = 1000, β = 0.019, R_i = 10 kΩ, R_o = 2 kΩ, f_H = 20 kHz
1 + Aβ = 1 + 19 = 20  (26 dB of feedback)
A_f = 1000/20 = 50
If A falls 20 % to 800: A_f = 800/(1 + 15.2) = 49.4, only 1.2 % lower
f_Hf = 20 kHz × 20 = 400 kHz  (gain × bandwidth: 1000 × 20k = 50 × 400k)
R_if = 10 kΩ × 20 = 200 kΩ,  R_of = 2 kΩ/20 = 100 Ω

Worked example 3: two-stage cascade with loading
R_s = 10 kΩ; stage 1: R_i1 = 50 kΩ, A_vo1 = 40, R_o1 = 4 kΩ
stage 2: R_i2 = 12 kΩ, A_vo2 = 25, R_o2 = 500 Ω; R_L = 2 kΩ
Input divider      50/(50 + 10)   = 0.833
Interstage divider 12/(12 + 4)    = 0.75
Output divider     2/(2 + 0.5)    = 0.8
v_o/v_s = 0.833 × 40 × 0.75 × 25 × 0.8 = 500  ->  54 dB
Unloaded product 40 × 25 = 1000 (60 dB): loading costs 6 dB

Common slips: multiplying open-circuit gains without the divider factors at each interface; using Aβ instead of 1 + Aβ for the amount of feedback; applying 20 log to a power ratio; and assuming feedback raises the input resistance in every case. Series mixing at the input raises R_i, shunt mixing lowers it; voltage sampling at the output lowers R_o, current sampling raises it.

notes.text: Memorise the class table as a chant: A 360° 25/50 %, B 180° 78.5 %, AB in between, C under 180° for RF, D switching above 90 %. Most amplifier MCQs are answered from one of those rows.
Voltage and current gains use 20 log, power gain uses 10 log. A ratio of 100 is 40 dB as a voltage gain but only 20 dB as a power gain; mixing the two is the most common decibel mistake.

The class letters rank neither quality nor age. They describe only the bias condition of the output device, so a class C stage can be the right choice (RF) even though its collector current is a train of pulses.

formulas.title: Voltage gain in dB
formulas.description: V_o and V_i are the output and input voltage amplitudes; the same 20 log rule applies to current gain, and a negative result means attenuation.

formulas.title: Power gain in dB
formulas.description: P_o and P_i are the output and input signal powers; use 10 log because power is proportional to the square of voltage.

flashcards.front: Where does the extra signal power at an amplifier's output come from?
flashcards.back: From the DC power supply. The active device uses the small input signal to control the flow of DC power into the load.

flashcards.front: List the conduction angles of classes A, B, AB and C.
flashcards.back: A: 360°; B: 180°; AB: between 180° and 360°; C: less than 180°. Class D is a switching amplifier and is not defined by a conduction angle.

flashcards.front: Which classes are used for audio power, RF power and battery-powered audio?
flashcards.back: Audio power: class AB (low distortion, good efficiency). RF power: class C with a tuned load. Battery devices: class D (above 90 % efficiency).

questions.questionText: The additional signal power that appears at the output of an amplifier is supplied by:
options: Charge stored in the transistor junctions
questions.explanation: An amplifier does not create energy. The input signal only controls the active device, which converts DC power from the supply into a larger AC signal in the load.

questions.questionText: Power amplifiers are grouped into classes A, B, AB and C according to:
options: The portion of the input cycle during which the output device conducts
The number of transistors in the output stage
questions.explanation: The class is fixed by the Q-point position, which sets the conduction angle: 360° for A, 180° for B, between 180° and 360° for AB and less than 180° for C.

questions.questionText: An amplifier has a voltage gain of 100. Expressed in decibels this is:
questions.explanation: Voltage gain in dB = 20 log10(100) = 20 × 2 = 40 dB. Only a power ratio of 100 would be 20 dB.

questions.questionText: Which amplifier class operates its output transistors as fully ON or fully OFF switches driven by a pulse-width-modulated signal?
questions.explanation: In class D the devices switch between saturation and cut-off at a high rate; the PWM pulse train is then low-pass filtered to recover the amplified signal, giving efficiencies above 90 %.

questions.questionText: The gain of a transconductance amplifier is measured in:
questions.explanation: A transconductance amplifier gives an output current for an input voltage, so G_m = i_o/v_i has units of amperes per volt, that is siemens.

questions.questionText: An amplifier that accepts an input current and delivers a proportional output voltage is a:
questions.explanation: Its gain R_m = v_o/i_i has units of volts per ampere (ohms), hence transresistance. A transconductance amplifier does the reverse.

questions.questionText: An ideal transconductance amplifier should have:
options: Zero input resistance and zero output resistance
Infinite input resistance and zero output resistance
Infinite input resistance and infinite output resistance
Zero input resistance and infinite output resistance
questions.explanation: It senses a voltage, so it should draw no input current (R_i infinite), and it delivers a current, so the output should behave as an ideal current source (R_o infinite).

questions.questionText: Applying negative feedback to an amplifier:
options: Increases its gain and narrows its bandwidth
Reduces its gain but makes the gain more stable
questions.explanation: A_f = A/(1 + Aβ) is smaller than A, but it depends much less on A, so the gain is desensitised to device changes. Bandwidth widens and distortion falls.

questions.questionText: Positive (regenerative) feedback is used deliberately in:
questions.explanation: Positive feedback increases the loop gain until the circuit oscillates or snaps between states. Amplifiers that need stable, low-distortion gain use negative feedback.

questions.questionText: An amplifier has a power gain of 30 dB. The output power is how many times the input power?
questions.explanation: Power ratio = 10^(dB/10) = 10^(30/10) = 1000. The value 31.6 is 10^(30/20), which would be a voltage ratio.

questions.questionText: An attenuator network halves the signal voltage. Its gain expressed in decibels is approximately:
questions.explanation: Gain = 20 log10(0.5) = −6.02 dB. −3 dB corresponds to halving the power, which is a voltage ratio of 0.707.

questions.questionText: An amplifier gives different gains to the different frequency components of a complex input signal, so the output waveform shape differs from the input although no new frequencies are created. This defect is called:
questions.explanation: Unequal gain across the band is frequency (amplitude-frequency) distortion, caused by the amplifier's limited bandwidth. Harmonic and intermodulation distortion come from non-linearity and create new frequencies; crossover distortion is a class B output-stage defect.

questions.questionText: For a given amplifying device, the product of mid-band gain and bandwidth is:
options: Approximately constant, so raising the gain widens the bandwidth
Proportional to the square of the bandwidth
Approximately constant, so raising the gain narrows the bandwidth
questions.explanation: The gain-bandwidth product is roughly fixed by the device, so gain can be traded for bandwidth: negative feedback that lowers the gain by a factor widens the bandwidth by the same factor.

questions.questionText: A power level quoted in dBm is expressed relative to:
questions.explanation: dBm = 10 log10(P/1 mW), so 0 dBm = 1 mW, 10 dBm = 10 mW and 30 dBm = 1 W.

questions.questionText: A voltage gain of −50 means that the output voltage is:
options: 50 times the input and inverted (180° phase shift)
questions.explanation: The magnitude 50 gives the amplification and the minus sign indicates phase inversion, as in a common-emitter or common-source stage.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT an effect of negative feedback?
options: Reduced sensitivity to changes in transistor parameters
questions.explanation: Negative feedback always divides the gain by 1 + Aβ. Wider bandwidth, lower distortion and desensitised gain are its benefits.

questions.questionText: A voltage amplifier is designed so that its input resistance is much larger than the source resistance. This ensures that:
options: The amplifier draws maximum current from the source
The amplifier output resistance becomes small
The bandwidth of the amplifier increases
Almost all of the source voltage appears across the amplifier input
questions.explanation: R_s and R_i form a divider, so v_i = v_s R_i/(R_i + R_s); with R_i >> R_s, v_i ≈ v_s and little signal is lost at the input.

questions.questionText: In voltage-series (series-shunt) negative feedback, the feedback signal is:
options: Sampled from the output current and applied in shunt with the input
Sampled from the output voltage and applied in shunt with the input
Sampled from the output voltage and applied in series with the input
Sampled from the output current and applied in series with the input
questions.explanation: The first word names the output quantity sampled (voltage, by a shunt connection) and the second the way it is mixed at the input (series). This topology gives a stabilised voltage amplifier.

questions.questionText: A voltage amplifier has A_vo = 200, R_i = 20 kΩ and R_o = 2 kΩ. It is fed from a source of resistance 5 kΩ and drives an 8 kΩ load. The overall voltage gain v_o/v_s is:
questions.explanation: v_o/v_s = [20/(20 + 5)] × 200 × [8/(8 + 2)] = 0.8 × 200 × 0.8 = 128. Including only one of the two dividers gives 160.

questions.questionText: An amplifier has an open-circuit output voltage of 6 V and an output resistance of 600 Ω. With a 600 Ω load connected, the output voltage is:
questions.explanation: The load and output resistances divide the internal voltage: V_L = 6 × 600/(600 + 600) = 3 V. This is the matched (maximum-power) condition.

questions.questionText: An amplifier's output voltage is 5 V on open circuit and falls to 4 V when a 1 kΩ load is connected. Its output resistance is:
questions.explanation: 4 = 5 × 1k/(1k + R_o) gives R_o = 1k × (5/4 − 1) = 250 Ω. Dividing the 1 V drop by the 5 V would wrongly give 200 Ω.

questions.questionText: A 10 mV source with an internal resistance of 10 kΩ is connected to an amplifier, and the voltage measured across the amplifier input is 8 mV. The amplifier input resistance is:
questions.explanation: The 2 mV lost across R_s gives the current 2 mV/10 kΩ = 0.2 µA, so R_i = 8 mV/0.2 µA = 40 kΩ.

questions.questionText: A transconductance amplifier with G_m = 10 mS and very high output resistance drives a 2 kΩ load. Its voltage gain v_o/v_i is:
questions.explanation: The output current is G_m v_i, which flows through R_L, so v_o/v_i = G_m R_L = 10 mS × 2 kΩ = 20.

questions.questionText: A transresistance amplifier has R_m = 10 kΩ and very low output resistance. For an input signal current of 50 µA, the output voltage is:
questions.explanation: v_o = R_m i_i = 10 kΩ × 50 µA = 0.5 V; with low R_o the load has no effect on this value.

questions.questionText: A voltage-amplifier model has A_vo = 100 and R_o = 5 kΩ. The short-circuit transconductance G_m of the equivalent Norton (transconductance) model is:
questions.explanation: Shorting the output gives i_sc = A_vo v_i/R_o, so G_m = A_vo/R_o = 100/5 kΩ = 20 mS, with the same R_o in parallel with the current source.

questions.questionText: A 10 dBm signal is applied to an amplifier with a power gain of 20 dB. The output power is:
questions.explanation: Decibels add: 10 dBm + 20 dB = 30 dBm, and P = 1 mW × 10^(30/10) = 1 W.

questions.questionText: An amplifier with a constant gain-bandwidth product of 1 MHz is set to a mid-band voltage gain of 40 dB. Its bandwidth is approximately:
questions.explanation: 40 dB is a gain of 100, so BW = GBW/A = 1 MHz/100 = 10 kHz. Dividing by 40 instead of by 100 gives 25 kHz.

questions.questionText: An amplifier with open-loop gain A = 500 is given negative feedback with β = 0.02. The closed-loop gain is approximately:
questions.explanation: A_f = A/(1 + Aβ) = 500/(1 + 10) = 45.5. The value 50 is the 1/β approximation, which is not accurate here because Aβ is only 10; 55.6 uses 1 − Aβ.

questions.questionText: An amplifier with A = 10 000 has negative feedback with β = 0.01. The amount of feedback, 20 log(1 + Aβ), is approximately:
questions.explanation: 1 + Aβ = 1 + 100 = 101, and 20 log10(101) = 40.1 dB, so the gain is reduced from 80 dB to about 40 dB.

questions.questionText: An amplifier with A = 1000 and upper cut-off frequency 10 kHz is given negative feedback with β = 0.009. The new upper cut-off frequency is:
questions.explanation: 1 + Aβ = 1 + 9 = 10, so f_Hf = f_H(1 + Aβ) = 10 kHz × 10 = 100 kHz, while the gain falls to 1000/10 = 100.

questions.questionText: A feedback amplifier has 1 + Aβ = 20. If the open-loop gain changes by 10 %, the closed-loop gain changes by about:
questions.explanation: dA_f/A_f = (dA/A)/(1 + Aβ) = 10 %/20 = 0.5 %. This desensitivity is the main reason for using negative feedback.

questions.questionText: Which feedback topology is used to build a stable transresistance amplifier?
questions.explanation: A transresistance amplifier takes a current in (shunt mixing, low R_i) and gives a voltage out (voltage sampling, low R_o), which is shunt-shunt feedback.

questions.questionText: Voltage-series negative feedback changes the input and output resistances of an amplifier as follows:
options: Both input and output resistance decrease
Input resistance increases and output resistance decreases
Both input and output resistance increase
Input resistance decreases and output resistance increases
questions.explanation: Series mixing multiplies R_i by 1 + Aβ and voltage sampling divides R_o by 1 + Aβ, moving the circuit towards an ideal voltage amplifier.

questions.questionText: Current-series (series-series) negative feedback:
options: Increases both the input and the output resistance
Increases the input resistance but decreases the output resistance
Decreases the input resistance but increases the output resistance
Decreases both the input and the output resistance
questions.explanation: Series mixing raises R_i and current sampling raises R_o, each by 1 + Aβ; this suits a transconductance amplifier, whose ideal R_i and R_o are both infinite.

questions.questionText: Which statement about cascaded amplifier stages is NOT correct?
options: The overall bandwidth of several identical stages is wider than that of one stage
The overall linear gain is the product of the loaded stage gains
The overall gain in decibels is the sum of the stage gains in decibels
The first stage has the greatest effect on the overall noise
questions.explanation: Each stage adds its own roll-off, so the bandwidth of a cascade is narrower than that of a single stage. The other statements are correct.

questions.questionText: Two identical non-interacting stages, each with an upper cut-off frequency of 100 kHz, are cascaded. The overall upper cut-off frequency is approximately:
questions.explanation: f_H(overall) = f_H √(2^(1/n) − 1) = 100 kHz × √(1.414 − 1) = 100 kHz × 0.644 = 64.4 kHz. Halving the bandwidth (50 kHz) overestimates the reduction.

questions.questionText: An amplifier's high-frequency response is set by a single RC low-pass section. At its upper cut-off frequency f_H, the phase of the output relative to its mid-band phase is shifted by:
questions.explanation: For a single-pole response the extra phase shift is −arctan(f/f_H), which equals −arctan(1) = −45° at f = f_H. It approaches −90° only when f is far above f_H.

questions.questionText: An amplifier takes an input of 10 mV across its 1 kΩ input resistance and produces 1 V across a 100 Ω load. Its power gain is:
questions.explanation: P_i = (10 mV)²/1 kΩ = 0.1 µW and P_o = (1 V)²/100 Ω = 10 mW, so A_p = 10^5 = 50 dB. 40 dB is the voltage gain, which equals the power gain only when the two resistances are equal.

questions.questionText: A source with high internal resistance must drive a low-resistance load without losing signal. The stage placed between them should have:
options: Low input resistance and high output resistance
Low input and low output resistance
High input resistance and low output resistance
High input and high output resistance
questions.explanation: High R_i avoids loading the source and low R_o avoids losing signal in the load divider; this is the role of a buffer such as an emitter follower.

questions.questionText: In a negative-feedback amplifier with loop gain Aβ >> 1, the closed-loop gain is approximately:
options: 1/β, set by the feedback network alone
questions.explanation: A_f = A/(1 + Aβ) → A/(Aβ) = 1/β when Aβ >> 1. Precision resistors in the feedback network therefore fix the gain.

questions.questionText: An amplifier with A = 100 produces 10 % second-harmonic distortion. Negative feedback with β = 0.04 is added and the input is raised to give the same output level. The distortion becomes:
questions.explanation: Distortion generated inside the loop is divided by 1 + Aβ = 1 + 4 = 5, so it falls from 10 % to 2 %.

questions.questionText: An amplifier has A = 200, R_i = 5 kΩ and R_o = 2 kΩ. Voltage-series negative feedback with β = 0.05 is applied. The input and output resistances with feedback are:
questions.explanation: 1 + Aβ = 1 + 10 = 11. Series mixing gives R_if = 5 kΩ × 11 = 55 kΩ, and voltage sampling gives R_of = 2 kΩ/11 = 182 Ω. Using Aβ = 10 instead of 11 gives 50 kΩ and 200 Ω.

questions.questionText: A voltage amplifier with A_vo = 500, R_i = 4 kΩ and R_o = 100 Ω is driven from a 1 kΩ source and feeds a 400 Ω load. The overall voltage gain v_o/v_s in decibels is approximately:
Stage 1 (A_vo1 = 50, R_i1 = 10 kΩ, R_o1 = 5 kΩ) drives stage 2 (A_vo2 = 40, R_i2 = 5 kΩ, R_o2 = 1 kΩ), which feeds a 4 kΩ load. The source is ideal (zero resistance). The overall voltage gain is:
questions.explanation: Interstage divider 5/(5 + 5) = 0.5 and output divider 4/(4 + 1) = 0.8, so A = 50 × 0.5 × 40 × 0.8 = 800. Ignoring loading gives 2000.

questions.questionText: An amplifier with A = 2000 has negative feedback with β = 0.05. If ageing reduces A to 1000 (a 50 % drop), the closed-loop gain falls by about:
questions.explanation: Before: A_f = 2000/(1 + 100) = 19.80. After: A_f = 1000/(1 + 50) = 19.61. The change is 0.19/19.80 ≈ 0.98 %, although A itself halved.

questions.questionText: An amplifier with open-loop gain A = 100 must have a closed-loop gain of 20 using negative feedback. The feedback fraction β required is:
questions.explanation: 20 = 100/(1 + 100β) gives 1 + 100β = 5, so β = 0.04. The value 0.05 comes from the 1/β approximation, which is poor when Aβ is only 4.

questions.questionText: An RC-coupled amplifier has A = 500, f_L = 50 Hz and f_H = 50 kHz. Negative feedback with β = 0.018 is applied. The new lower and upper cut-off frequencies are:
questions.explanation: 1 + Aβ = 1 + 9 = 10. Feedback divides f_L and multiplies f_H by this factor: f_Lf = 50/10 = 5 Hz and f_Hf = 50 kHz × 10 = 500 kHz, while the gain drops to 50.

questions.questionText: A current amplifier (A_is = 100, R_i = 100 Ω, R_o = 10 kΩ) is driven by a Norton source of 10 µA in parallel with 900 Ω and feeds a 1 kΩ load. The overall current gain i_o/i_s is approximately:
questions.explanation: Input current division: i_i = i_s × 900/(900 + 100) = 0.9i_s. Output division: i_o = 100i_i × 10k/(10k + 1k) = 90.9i_i. Overall 0.9 × 100 × 0.909 = 81.8.

questions.questionText: A 1 mW signal passes through a pre-amplifier with 20 dB gain, a cable with 6 dB loss and a power amplifier with 30 dB gain. The output power is approximately:
questions.explanation: Input is 0 dBm; output = 0 + 20 − 6 + 30 = 44 dBm, so P = 1 mW × 10^4.4 = 25.1 W.

questions.questionText: A transconductance amplifier has G_m = 20 mS, a very high input resistance and an output resistance of 10 kΩ. With a 10 kΩ load, its voltage gain v_o/v_i is:
questions.explanation: The output current G_m v_i divides between R_o and R_L, so v_o = G_m v_i (R_o ∥ R_L) = 20 mS × 5 kΩ × v_i, giving a gain of 100. Ignoring R_o gives 200.

subtopics.title: Amplifier Basics
subtopics.subtitle: Gain in dB, impedances, bandwidth, distortion, efficiency, coupling and cascading

concepts.text: Gain and Decibels

Voltage gain A_v is the ratio of output to input voltage, current gain A_i the ratio of output to input current, and power gain A_p the ratio of output to input signal power. Because P = VI, the power gain equals the product of the voltage and current gains. All three are dimensionless: a gain greater than 1 means amplification and a gain less than 1 means attenuation. A common-emitter stage has both voltage and current gain, an emitter follower has current gain only (A_v about 1), and a common-base stage has voltage gain only (A_i slightly below 1).

concepts.plainText: Av = Vo/Vi, Ai = Io/Ii, Ap = Po/Pi = Av × Ai

concepts.text: Gains are usually quoted in decibels (dB), a logarithmic unit that turns multiplication into addition and compresses very wide ranges. Power gain in dB is 10 log10(P_o/P_i). Because power is proportional to the square of voltage (P = V²/R), a voltage or current ratio is converted with 20 log10; strictly this equals the power gain only when the input and output resistances are equal, but the 20 log convention is applied to every voltage ratio regardless. A gain below 1 gives negative decibels (a loss). The point at which the gain has fallen by 3 dB is the half-power point: power is halved and voltage is 0.707 of its mid-band value.

Worked example. A two-stage amplifier has voltage gains of 20 and 50. The overall gain is 20 × 50 = 1000, that is 20 log10(1000) = 60 dB; the same answer comes from adding the stage gains, 20 log 20 = 26 dB and 20 log 50 = 34 dB. If that amplifier raises 10 mW of input power to 1 W, the power gain is 100, which is 10 log10(100) = 20 dB, not 40 dB.
Impedances and Bandwidth
Z_in is the impedance the amplifier presents to its source and Z_out is the Thevenin impedance it presents to the load. The ideal values depend on which quantity the amplifier must preserve:
items: Voltage amplifier: Z_in infinite (draws no current from the source, so no signal is lost across the source resistance) and Z_out zero (the full output voltage reaches any load). Practical designs aim for high Z_in and low Z_out, as in an emitter follower or an op-amp.
Current amplifier: Z_in zero (all of the source current enters) and Z_out infinite (the same current is delivered to any load).
Transconductance amplifier (voltage in, current out): Z_in infinite and Z_out infinite. Transresistance amplifier (current in, voltage out): both zero.
For maximum power transfer between stages, Z_out of one stage should equal Z_in of the next; transformer coupling is used when this matching matters, for example at a loudspeaker or antenna.

concepts.text: The frequency response is a plot of gain (usually in dB) against frequency on a logarithmic axis. For an RC-coupled amplifier it is flat over the mid-band, falls at low frequencies because coupling and bypass capacitors present increasing reactance, and falls at high frequencies because junction capacitances, stray wiring capacitance (multiplied by the Miller effect) and the finite transit time of carriers shunt the signal. The lower cut-off f_L and upper cut-off f_H are the frequencies at which the gain drops to 0.707 of the mid-band value (−3 dB, half power), and the bandwidth is their difference; a direct-coupled amplifier has f_L = 0, so its bandwidth simply equals f_H. For a given device the gain-bandwidth product is roughly constant, so more gain per stage means less bandwidth.

concepts.plainText: BW = fH − fL; |A| at cut-off = A_mid/√2 = 0.707 A_mid

concepts.text: Distortion and Efficiency
Any change in the shape of the signal other than a scale factor is distortion:
items: Amplitude (non-linear or harmonic) distortion: the transfer characteristic of the device is not a straight line, so a pure sine input produces new frequencies at 2f, 3f and so on. It is measured as total harmonic distortion (THD) and is worst for large signals and for a Q-point near saturation or cut-off.
Frequency distortion: different frequency components are amplified by different amounts because of reactive elements, so a complex waveform changes shape even though no new frequencies are created.
Phase (delay) distortion: the phase shift is not proportional to frequency, so components arrive with different delays; it matters for video and pulse signals but is inaudible in audio.

Intermodulation distortion: two input frequencies generate sum and difference products. Crossover distortion in class B stages is a special case of non-linear distortion and is treated in the next subtopics.

concepts.text: The conversion efficiency of a power amplifier is the AC signal power delivered to the load divided by the DC power taken from the supply, where P_dc equals the supply voltage times the average supply current. Whatever is not delivered to the load is dissipated as heat in the transistor (and in any collector resistor), so P_D = P_dc − P_ac. Efficiency is the property that separates the amplifier classes: a class A stage draws its full supply current even with no signal, while a class B stage draws current only while a signal is present.
Coupling Methods and Cascading

rows: Flat over the audio band; poor at low frequencies because of coupling-capacitor reactance
No matching; DC power is wasted in the collector resistor
Small-signal audio and voltage-amplifier stages; cheap and compact
Poor and non-flat; winding resonance and core losses limit the band
Excellent matching through the turns ratio; higher efficiency because no DC is dropped in the load
Power-amplifier outputs and tuned RF stages; bulky and costly
Extends down to DC (f_L = 0); no reactive components
No matching; the bias of one stage affects the next and drifts with temperature

concepts.text: When stages are cascaded the overall gain is the product of the individual gains (each measured with the next stage connected as its load), so gains in decibels simply add. Bandwidth shrinks as stages are added because every stage contributes its own roll-off; for n identical stages the overall upper cut-off is f_H √(2^(1/n) − 1). Noise generated in the first stage is amplified by every following stage, so the input stage must be the low-noise one; later stages contribute little to the output noise.
Going Deeper: Small-Signal Amplifier Configurations

Small-signal analysis replaces the transistor by a linear model valid for small swings about the Q-point. For a BJT the simplest is the r_e model: the base-emitter junction looks like a resistance r_e = V_T/I_E seen from the emitter (about 25 Ω at 1 mA with V_T = 25 mV), and β r_e seen from the base, while the collector acts as a current source of α i_e. A signal voltage v_b at the base therefore drives an emitter current v_b/(r_e + R_E), where R_E is any unbypassed emitter resistance, and nearly all of that current flows through the collector load. The CE voltage gain is simply the ratio of the total collector load resistance to the total emitter-circuit resistance, with a minus sign for the 180° phase inversion.

concepts.plainText: Av = −(RC || RL)/(re + RE), with re = VT/IE; Rin(base) = β(re + RE)

concepts.text: An FET is modelled by a transconductance g_m from gate voltage to drain current, with an open-circuit gate. The common-source gain is −g_m (R_D ∥ R_L), and the source follower (common drain) gives g_m R_S/(1 + g_m R_S), always below 1, with an output resistance of R_S ∥ 1/g_m. For a JFET, g_m = g_m0 (1 − V_GS/V_P) with g_m0 = 2 I_DSS/|V_P|; for a MOSFET in saturation g_m = 2 I_D/(V_GS − V_t). Because g_m of an FET at a few milliamperes is far lower than the 40 mA/V per milliampere of a BJT, FET stages give less voltage gain but offer a practically infinite input resistance.

rows: Set by the gate bias resistor, very high

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: divider-biased CE stage, beta = 120, VT = 25 mV
VCC = 15 V, R1 = 56 k, R2 = 12 k, RC = 3.3 k, RE = 1 k (bypassed), RL = 10 k
VB = 15 x 12/(56 + 12) = 2.65 V ;  VE = 2.65 - 0.7 = 1.95 V
IE = 1.95 V / 1 k = 1.95 mA ;  re = 25 mV / 1.95 mA = 12.8 ohm
beta re = 120 x 12.8 = 1.54 k
Rin = R1 || R2 || beta re = 9.88 k || 1.54 k = 1.33 k
Av = -(RC || RL)/re = -(2.48 k)/12.8 = -193
With RE unbypassed: Av = -2.48 k/(1012.8) = -2.45 only

Each coupling capacitor forms a high-pass section with the resistance it sees: the input capacitor with R_s + R_in, the output capacitor with R_C + R_L. The emitter bypass capacitor is usually the one that sets f_L, because the resistance it sees looking into the emitter is tiny, R_E ∥ (r_e + R_s'/β), so it needs a much larger capacitance for the same cut-off. At high frequencies the device capacitances take over. Miller's theorem shows that a capacitance C_μ (C_bc) bridging an inverting stage of gain −A behaves at the input like C_μ(1 + A), so a small feedback capacitance becomes the dominant input capacitance and sets f_H.

concepts.plainText: fL = 1/(2π(Rs + Rin)Cc); Miller input capacitance CM = Cμ(1 + |Av|); then fH = 1/(2π Rth Cin)

concepts.text:
Worked example 2: cut-off frequencies of the stage in example 1
Input coupling C1 = 10 uF, source resistance Rs = 600 ohm
fL(C1) = 1/(2 pi (600 + 1333) x 10e-6) = 8.2 Hz
High end: C_pi = 15 pF, C_mu = 3 pF, gain from base = -(RC || RL)/re = -193
Miller: C_in = 15 + 3 x (1 + 193) = 597 pF
Thevenin resistance driving the base Rth = Rs || Rin = 600 || 1333 = 414 ohm
fH = 1/(2 pi x 414 x 597e-12) = 644 kHz
Without Miller multiplication (18 pF) fH would wrongly come out near 21 MHz

When stages are cascaded, each stage's gain must be found with the next stage's input resistance as its load, and the first stage's input resistance loads the source. A practical method treats every stage as a Thevenin source of open-circuit gain A_oc and output resistance R_o, then multiplies the voltage-divider losses R_in(next)/(R_o + R_in(next)) at each interface. Buffers (emitter or source followers) are placed where a high-impedance stage must drive a low-impedance load, and the cascode (CE followed by CB) removes the Miller multiplication because the CE stage then sees only the tiny r_e of the CB stage as its load.

Common slips: forgetting R_L in parallel with R_C; using β r_e instead of r_e in the gain formula; ignoring the bias resistors R1 ∥ R2 when finding the stage input resistance; using the open-circuit gain of a stage while it is loaded by the next stage; and multiplying C_μ by A instead of (1 + A) for the Miller capacitance.

Quick checks: CE gain ≈ R_C/r_e bypassed or R_C/R_E unbypassed; follower gain just under 1; CB input resistance ≈ r_e. For n identical stages the overall f_H is f_H √(2^(1/n) − 1) and the overall f_L is f_L/√(2^(1/n) − 1): 0.644 for two stages and 0.510 for three.

formulas.plainText: η = P_ac / P_dc × 100 %; P_D = P_dc − P_ac

formulas.latex: A_T = A_1 A_2 \cdots A_n, \quad A_T(\text{dB}) = \sum A_k(\text{dB})
formulas.plainText: A_total = A1 × A2 × ... × An; A_total(dB) = sum of stage gains in dB

notes.text: Half-power point: −3 dB, power halves, voltage falls to 0.707 (1/√2). Questions often ask between which points bandwidth is measured: the answer is where gain falls to 70.7 % of its maximum.
Decibel gains of cascaded stages add; linear gains multiply. Never multiply decibels, and never add linear gains.
20 log(V_o/V_i) equals the power gain in dB only when the input and output resistances are equal; the exam nevertheless expects 20 log for any voltage ratio and 10 log for any power ratio.

Ideal voltage amplifier: Z_in infinite, Z_out zero. Ideal current amplifier: the reverse. Remember it as: a voltage amplifier wants no current drawn at its input, a current amplifier wants no voltage dropped there.

formulas.title: Voltage and current gain in dB
formulas.description: Use for any ratio of voltages or currents; 20 appears because power is proportional to the square of these quantities.

formulas.title: Power gain in dB
formulas.description: P_o and P_i are output and input signal powers; a power ratio of 2 is 3 dB and of 10 is 10 dB.

formulas.title: Bandwidth and half-power points
formulas.description: f_L and f_H are the lower and upper cut-off frequencies where gain is 3 dB (a factor 0.707) below the mid-band value A_mid.

formulas.title: Efficiency and dissipation
formulas.plainText: η = P_ac / P_dc × 100 %; P_D = P_dc − P_ac
formulas.description: P_ac is signal power in the load, P_dc = V_CC × average supply current, and P_D is the heat dissipated in the output device.

formulas.title: Cascaded stages
formulas.latex: A_T = A_1 A_2 \cdots A_n, \quad A_T(\text{dB}) = \sum A_k(\text{dB})
formulas.plainText: A_total = A1 × A2 × ... × An; A_total(dB) = A1(dB) + A2(dB) + ...
formulas.description: Linear gains of stages in cascade multiply while decibel gains add; each A_k must be measured with the following stage as its load.

flashcards.front: Why is 20 log used for voltage gain but 10 log for power gain?
flashcards.back: Power is proportional to V², so 10 log(V_o²/V_i²) = 20 log(V_o/V_i). The 20 log rule is applied to any voltage or current ratio.

flashcards.front: Define the bandwidth of an amplifier.
flashcards.back: BW = f_H − f_L, where f_L and f_H are the frequencies at which the gain falls to 0.707 (−3 dB, half power) of its mid-band value.

flashcards.front: What limits the low- and high-frequency response of an RC-coupled amplifier?
flashcards.back: Low end: coupling and bypass capacitors. High end: junction and stray (Miller) capacitances and carrier transit time.

flashcards.front: Name the three classical types of distortion in an amplifier.
flashcards.back: Amplitude (harmonic or non-linear) distortion, frequency distortion and phase (delay) distortion.

questions.questionText: An amplifier delivers 1 W to its load for a signal input power of 10 mW. Its power gain in decibels is:
questions.explanation: Power ratio = 1 W / 10 mW = 100; A_p(dB) = 10 log10(100) = 20 dB. Using 20 log (the voltage rule) would wrongly give 40 dB.

questions.questionText: An ideal voltage amplifier should have:
options: Zero input impedance and infinite output impedance
Zero input impedance and zero output impedance
Infinite input impedance and zero output impedance
Infinite input impedance and infinite output impedance
questions.explanation: Infinite Z_in means no signal is lost across the source resistance; zero Z_out means the full output voltage appears across any load.

questions.questionText: The bandwidth of an amplifier is measured between the frequencies at which the voltage gain falls to what fraction of its mid-band value?
questions.explanation: The cut-off frequencies are the −3 dB (half-power) points, where voltage gain is 1/√2 = 0.707 of the mid-band gain. 50 % refers to power, not voltage.

questions.questionText: Three identical stages, each with a voltage gain of 10, are cascaded. The overall voltage gain in decibels is:
questions.explanation: Each stage gives 20 log10(10) = 20 dB and decibel gains add: 3 × 20 = 60 dB, equivalent to a linear gain of 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000.

questions.questionText: A common-emitter stage has a voltage gain of −150. The magnitude of its gain in decibels is approximately:
questions.explanation: |A_v|(dB) = 20 log10(150) = 43.5 dB. The minus sign only indicates the 180° phase inversion; 10 log would give 21.8 dB, which applies to power ratios.

questions.questionText: For a sinusoidal input, the output voltage of a common-emitter amplifier is:
options: 180° out of phase with the input
questions.explanation: An increase in base voltage increases the collector current, which increases the drop across R_C and lowers the collector voltage, so the output is inverted (180° phase shift) in the mid-band.

questions.questionText: Which BJT configuration is normally used as a buffer between a high-resistance source and a low-resistance load?
options: Common emitter with unbypassed emitter resistor
questions.explanation: The emitter follower has a high input resistance, a low output resistance and a voltage gain close to 1, which is exactly what a buffer needs.

questions.questionText: A common-base amplifier stage has:
options: High input resistance, low output resistance and voltage gain slightly less than 1
High input resistance, high output resistance and current gain equal to β
Low input resistance, low output resistance and a voltage gain of −β
Low input resistance, high output resistance and current gain slightly less than 1
questions.explanation: In CB the signal enters at the emitter, so R_in ≈ r_e (tens of ohms); the collector looks like a high-resistance current source and the current gain is α, just below 1, while voltage gain can be large.

questions.questionText: A CE stage with a fully bypassed emitter resistor runs at I_E = 1 mA (take V_T = 25 mV). It has R_C = 4.7 kΩ and drives a load R_L = 4.7 kΩ. Its voltage gain is:
questions.explanation: r_e = 25 mV/1 mA = 25 Ω; A_v = −(R_C ∥ R_L)/r_e = −(2.35 kΩ)/25 Ω = −94. Ignoring R_L gives −188.

questions.questionText: A CE amplifier has R_C = 5 kΩ (no external load), an unbypassed emitter resistor R_E = 1 kΩ, and r_e = 25 Ω. Its voltage gain is approximately:
questions.explanation: With R_E unbypassed, A_v = −R_C/(r_e + R_E) = −5000/1025 = −4.9. The value −200 applies only if R_E were fully bypassed.

questions.questionText: Of the three BJT amplifier configurations, the one that provides the highest power gain is:
options: All three give the same power gain
questions.explanation: Power gain is A_v × A_i. The common-emitter stage has both a large voltage gain and a large current gain (about β), whereas the common base has A_i < 1 and the common collector has A_v < 1.

questions.questionText: A CE stage has β = 100, r_e = 25 Ω and an unbypassed emitter resistor of 470 Ω. The resistance looking into the base is approximately:
questions.explanation: R_in(base) = β(r_e + R_E) = 100 × 495 Ω = 49.5 kΩ. Forgetting the emitter resistor gives only β r_e = 2.5 kΩ.

questions.questionText: A voltage-divider biased CE stage has R1 = 47 kΩ, R2 = 10 kΩ, β = 150 and r_e = 26 Ω, with the emitter resistor fully bypassed. The input resistance of the stage seen by the signal source is approximately:
questions.explanation: β r_e = 150 × 26 = 3.9 kΩ and R1 ∥ R2 = 8.25 kΩ; R_in = 8.25 kΩ ∥ 3.9 kΩ = 2.65 kΩ. Adding R1, R2 and β r_e in series instead of paralleling them gives 60.9 kΩ.

questions.questionText: An emitter follower with β = 100, r_e = 25 Ω and R_E = 2 kΩ is driven from a source of effective resistance 1 kΩ. Its output resistance is approximately:
questions.explanation: Looking into the emitter the source resistance is divided by β: r_e + R_s/β = 25 + 10 = 35 Ω. In parallel with R_E: 2000 ∥ 35 = 34.4 Ω.

questions.questionText: Neglecting the transistor's output resistance r_o, the output resistance of a common-emitter stage is approximately equal to:
questions.explanation: The collector behaves as an ideal current source (infinite resistance), so the resistance seen at the output terminal is just R_C.

questions.questionText: A common-base stage has r_e = 25 Ω, R_C = 5 kΩ and a load of 5 kΩ. Its voltage gain and input resistance (at the emitter) are approximately:
questions.explanation: A_v = +(R_C ∥ R_L)/r_e = 2500/25 = +100 with no phase inversion, and the input resistance at the emitter is r_e = 25 Ω.

questions.questionText: A common-source MOSFET amplifier has g_m = 2 mS, R_D = 10 kΩ and a load R_L = 10 kΩ, with the source resistor bypassed. Its voltage gain is:
questions.explanation: A_v = −g_m (R_D ∥ R_L) = −2 mS × 5 kΩ = −10. Ignoring the load gives −20.

questions.questionText: A JFET has I_DSS = 10 mA and V_P = −4 V and is biased at V_GS = −1 V in a common-source stage with R_D = 2.2 kΩ, the source resistor bypassed and no external load. The voltage gain is approximately:
questions.explanation: g_m0 = 2I_DSS/|V_P| = 5 mS; g_m = g_m0(1 − V_GS/V_P) = 5 × 0.75 = 3.75 mS; A_v = −g_m R_D = −3.75 mS × 2.2 kΩ = −8.25. Using g_m0 directly gives −11.

questions.questionText: A common-source MOSFET stage has g_m = 4 mS, R_D = 6 kΩ, a load R_L = 6 kΩ and an unbypassed source resistor R_S = 500 Ω (r_o neglected). Its voltage gain is:
questions.explanation: The AC drain load is R_D ∥ R_L = 3 kΩ, and the unbypassed R_S divides the gain by (1 + g_m R_S) = 3: A_v = −(4 mS × 3 kΩ)/3 = −4. Ignoring R_S gives −12; the approximation −R_D'/R_S gives −6.

questions.questionText: The FET configuration that corresponds to the BJT emitter follower is the:
questions.explanation: In common drain the output is taken from the source, which follows the gate with a gain just below 1, exactly as the emitter follows the base in a common-collector stage.

questions.questionText: Among the three BJT configurations, the one with the highest input resistance is:
options: All three have the same input resistance
questions.explanation: The emitter follower's input resistance is (β + 1) times the total emitter resistance, far higher than β r_e (CE) or r_e (CB).

questions.questionText: The emitter bypass capacitor of a working CE amplifier becomes open-circuited. Which change results?
options: The voltage gain falls sharply while the input resistance rises
The voltage gain rises sharply while the input resistance falls
The DC Q-point shifts to saturation
The output becomes in phase with the input
questions.explanation: With C_E open, R_E appears in the signal path and gives negative feedback: gain falls from R_C/r_e to about R_C/(r_e + R_E), and R_in(base) rises to β(r_e + R_E). DC bias is unchanged because a capacitor carries no DC.

questions.questionText: A CE stage has R_E = 1 kΩ, r_e = 25 Ω, β = 100 and an effective source resistance (R_s ∥ R1 ∥ R2) of 1 kΩ. The bypass capacitor needed for a lower cut-off of 100 Hz due to C_E is approximately:
questions.explanation: Resistance seen by C_E = R_E ∥ (r_e + R_s'/β) = 1000 ∥ 35 = 33.8 Ω; C_E = 1/(2π × 33.8 × 100) = 47 µF. Using R_E alone gives only 1.6 µF.

questions.questionText: The input coupling capacitor of an amplifier is 1 µF. The source resistance is 600 Ω and the amplifier input resistance is 2.4 kΩ. The lower cut-off frequency due to this capacitor is approximately:
questions.explanation: The capacitor sees R_s + R_in = 3 kΩ: f_L = 1/(2π × 3000 × 1 µF) = 53 Hz. Leaving out 2π gives 333 Hz.

questions.questionText: The main purpose of the coupling capacitor between two RC-coupled stages is to:
options: Pass the signal while blocking the DC collector voltage of one stage from the base of the next
questions.explanation: The capacitor is a near short circuit for signal frequencies but an open circuit for DC, so each stage keeps its own bias point.

questions.questionText: The gain of an RC-coupled BJT amplifier falls at high frequencies mainly because of:
options: Junction and stray capacitances, magnified at the input by the Miller effect
The rising reactance of the coupling capacitors
The rising reactance of the emitter bypass capacitor
questions.explanation: At high frequency the shunting internal capacitances (C_π, and C_μ multiplied by the Miller effect) bypass the signal; coupling and bypass capacitors affect only the low-frequency end.

questions.questionText: An inverting amplifier stage with voltage gain −100 has a 2 pF capacitance connected between its input and output. The equivalent Miller capacitance seen at the input is:
questions.explanation: C_M = C(1 + |A|) = 2 pF × 101 = 202 pF. The value 2.02 pF is the output-side Miller capacitance C(1 + 1/|A|).

questions.questionText: A CE stage has C_π = 10 pF, C_μ = 2 pF and a mid-band gain from base to collector of −50. It is driven from a Thevenin resistance of 1 kΩ. The upper cut-off frequency set by the input circuit is approximately:
questions.explanation: C_in = C_π + C_μ(1 + 50) = 10 + 102 = 112 pF; f_H = 1/(2π × 1 kΩ × 112 pF) = 1.42 MHz. Ignoring the Miller effect (12 pF) wrongly gives 13.3 MHz.

questions.questionText: A common-base stage has a much wider bandwidth than a common-emitter stage using the same transistor because:
options: Its current gain is larger than β
The grounded base separates input from output, so C_bc is not multiplied by the Miller effect
It has a very high input resistance
Its voltage gain is always below 1
questions.explanation: In CB, C_bc sits from collector to ground (the base) rather than bridging an inverting gain from input to output, so there is no Miller multiplication of the input capacitance.

questions.questionText: The cascode connection (a CE stage followed by a CB stage) is used mainly to:
options: Obtain a voltage gain of exactly 1
Provide a very low input resistance
Remove the need for DC biasing
Obtain a wide bandwidth by suppressing the Miller effect in the CE stage
questions.explanation: The CE stage is loaded by the low r_e of the CB stage, so its own voltage gain is about −1 and C_μ is only doubled; the CB stage supplies the voltage gain without Miller multiplication.

questions.questionText: Stage 1 has an open-circuit voltage gain of 50 and output resistance 2 kΩ. It drives stage 2, which has input resistance 2 kΩ, open-circuit gain 20 and output resistance 1 kΩ. Stage 2 drives a 1 kΩ load. The overall voltage gain (ideal source) is:
questions.explanation: Interface losses: 2/(2 + 2) = 0.5 and 1/(1 + 1) = 0.5; A = 50 × 0.5 × 20 × 0.5 = 250. Ignoring loading gives 1000; adding the gains is never valid.

questions.questionText: A signal passes through a 20 dB amplifier, a 26 dB amplifier and a 6 dB attenuator (−6 dB) in cascade. The overall voltage gain as a plain ratio is approximately:
questions.explanation: Decibels add: 20 + 26 − 6 = 40 dB, and 40 dB is a voltage ratio of 10^(40/20) = 100.

questions.questionText: Three identical non-interacting RC-coupled stages each have an upper cut-off frequency of 300 kHz. The upper cut-off frequency of the cascade is approximately:
questions.explanation: f_H(overall) = f_H √(2^(1/3) − 1) = 300 × 0.510 = 153 kHz; bandwidth shrinks, but not simply in proportion to the number of stages.

questions.questionText: Two identical non-interacting RC-coupled stages each have a lower cut-off frequency of 40 Hz. The lower cut-off frequency of the two-stage amplifier is approximately:
questions.explanation: f_L(overall) = f_L/√(2^(1/2) − 1) = 40/0.644 = 62 Hz; the lower cut-off rises when stages are cascaded. Multiplying by 0.644 (26 Hz) is the rule for f_H, not f_L.

questions.questionText: An amplifier has a gain of 100 with a bandwidth of 50 kHz. If negative feedback reduces its gain to 20, keeping the gain-bandwidth product constant, the new bandwidth is:
questions.explanation: GBW = 100 × 50 kHz = 5 MHz; new bandwidth = 5 MHz/20 = 250 kHz.

questions.questionText: An audio amplifier has a lower cut-off frequency of 20 Hz and an upper cut-off frequency of 20 kHz. Its bandwidth is:
questions.explanation: BW = f_H − f_L = 20 000 − 20 = 19 980 Hz = 19.98 kHz; neither the average of the cut-offs (10.01 kHz) nor their ratio (1000) is the bandwidth.

questions.questionText: An amplifier has a mid-band voltage gain of 40 dB. Its voltage gain at the upper cut-off frequency, expressed as a plain ratio, is:
questions.explanation: 40 dB is a ratio of 100; at the −3 dB point the voltage gain is 100/√2 = 70.7. The number 37 is the gain in dB, not a ratio, and 50 wrongly halves the voltage.

questions.questionText: Which statement about the mid-band region of an RC-coupled amplifier is NOT correct?
options: Coupling and bypass capacitors act practically as short circuits
Internal junction capacitances act practically as open circuits
The gain is essentially independent of frequency
The gain is limited by the reactance of the coupling capacitors
questions.explanation: In the mid-band the coupling capacitors are effectively shorts and the small device capacitances are effectively open, so the gain is flat; coupling-capacitor reactance matters only below the mid-band.

questions.questionText: An emitter follower has β = 100 (use β + 1 = 101), r_e = 25 Ω, R_E = 1 kΩ and a load R_L = 1 kΩ coupled to the emitter. The resistance looking into the base is approximately:
questions.explanation: The emitter load is R_E ∥ R_L = 500 Ω, so R_in(base) = (β + 1)(r_e + 500) = 101 × 525 = 53 kΩ. Forgetting R_L gives 104 kΩ.

questions.questionText: An amplifier with input resistance 1 kΩ and voltage gain −100 (input terminals to output) is driven by a signal source of internal resistance 1 kΩ. The overall gain from source EMF to output is:
questions.explanation: Only R_in/(R_s + R_in) = 1/2 of the source EMF reaches the input, so A_vs = −100 × 0.5 = −50.

questions.questionText: An amplifier has a voltage gain of 50 and a current gain of 40. Its power gain in decibels is approximately:
questions.explanation: A_p = A_v × A_i = 2000, and A_p(dB) = 10 log10(2000) = 33 dB. Using 20 log gives 66 dB; adding the gains (90) gives 19.5 dB.

questions.questionText: A BJT stage has g_m = 40 mA/V, collector resistor R_C = 10 kΩ and transistor output resistance r_o = 40 kΩ, with no external load and the emitter bypassed. Its voltage gain is:
questions.explanation: The effective collector load is R_C ∥ r_o = 8 kΩ, so A_v = −g_m × 8 kΩ = −320. Neglecting r_o gives −400.

questions.questionText: Compared with a BJT common-emitter stage at a similar current, a MOSFET common-source stage typically has:
options: A lower input resistance and a higher voltage gain
A much higher input resistance but a lower voltage gain
A higher input resistance and a higher voltage gain
No phase inversion between input and output
questions.explanation: The insulated gate draws no current, so input resistance is huge, but an FET's g_m is much smaller than a BJT's I_C/V_T, so −g_m R_D is lower. Both stages invert.

questions.questionText: Which statement about an emitter follower is NOT correct?
options: Its output is in phase with its input
It has high input resistance and low output resistance
It provides a voltage gain much greater than 1
Its current gain is approximately β + 1
questions.explanation: The emitter follows the base with a gain slightly below 1; its value lies in current gain and impedance transformation, not voltage gain.

questions.questionText: A Darlington pair uses two transistors each with β = 80. Its overall current gain is approximately:
questions.explanation: The emitter current of the first transistor is the base current of the second, so β_D ≈ β1 × β2 = 80 × 80 = 6400.

questions.questionText: A CE amplifier has V_CC = 12 V, R1 = 40 kΩ, R2 = 10 kΩ, R_C = 4 kΩ, R_E = 1 kΩ (fully bypassed), no external load, and β large enough to ignore base current. Take V_BE = 0.7 V and V_T = 25 mV. The voltage gain is approximately:
questions.explanation: V_B = 12 × 10/50 = 2.4 V, I_E = (2.4 − 0.7)/1 kΩ = 1.7 mA, r_e = 25/1.7 = 14.7 Ω; A_v = −4000/14.7 = −272. Ignoring V_BE gives −384; forgetting the bypass gives −4.

questions.questionText: Which type of inter-stage coupling allows an amplifier to amplify signals down to zero frequency (DC)?
options: Capacitive coupling with a large emitter bypass capacitor
questions.explanation: A direct-coupled amplifier has no series capacitors or transformers, so f_L = 0; capacitors and transformers both block DC.

questions.questionText: A pure sine wave applied to an amplifier produces an output containing components at 2f and 3f as well as f. This is:
questions.explanation: New frequency components that are multiples of the input frequency come from a non-linear transfer characteristic, which is harmonic or amplitude distortion; frequency and phase distortion create no new frequencies.

questions.questionText: An amplifier's low-frequency response is set by a single RC section giving f_L = 100 Hz. Relative to mid-band, its gain at 50 Hz is approximately:
questions.explanation: |A/A_mid| = 1/√(1 + (f_L/f)²) = 1/√(1 + 4) = 0.447, which is 20 log(0.447) = −7.0 dB. Inverting the ratio (f/f_L) gives −0.97 dB.

questions.questionText: An amplifier with a voltage gain of 30 dB receives an input of 20 mV rms. The output voltage is approximately:
questions.explanation: Voltage ratio = 10^(30/20) = 31.6, so V_o = 31.6 × 20 mV = 632 mV. Using 10^(30/10) = 1000 wrongly gives 20 V.

subtopics.title: Classification of Output Stages
subtopics.subtitle: Q-point position on the load line fixes the conduction angle and hence the class

concepts.text: Load Line and Q-Point

The DC load line is drawn on the transistor's output characteristics between the point V_CE = V_CC (where I_C = 0) and the point I_C = V_CC/R_L (where V_CE = 0); every possible operating point for that supply and load lies on it. The bias network fixes the no-signal operating point, the Q-point (I_CQ, V_CEQ), and the input signal swings the instantaneous operating point along the line about Q. How far down the line the Q-point sits decides for what fraction of each input cycle the transistor carries current, its conduction angle, and that in turn defines the amplifier class.
Class A

The Q-point is placed at the centre of the load line, V_CEQ about V_CC/2 and I_CQ about V_CC/(2R_L), so the signal can swing equally towards saturation and cut-off without clipping. The transistor conducts for the full 360° of the cycle and the collector current is a complete sine wave riding on the steady I_CQ, so the output is the most faithful replica of the input. A single transistor is enough, with either a collector resistor (series-fed, RC coupled) or an output transformer as the load. The price is a constant supply current, and therefore heat, even when no signal is present.
Class B

The Q-point is at cut-off: I_CQ = 0 and V_CEQ = V_CC, so the transistor conducts only while the input drives it on, for 180° of each cycle, and its collector current is a series of half-sine pulses. Because one transistor reproduces only half the waveform, two are used in push-pull: one handles the positive half-cycle and the other the negative half, and the two halves are combined in an output transformer or, in a complementary-symmetry stage, at the joined emitters of an npn and a pnp transistor. Standby current is zero, but the hand-over between the two transistors produces crossover distortion.
Class AB

The Q-point is placed slightly above cut-off with a small quiescent current, typically a few milliamperes to a few tens of milliamperes. Each transistor then conducts for a little more than 180° (the conduction angle lies between 180° and 360°), so around the zero crossing both are on and the hand-over is smooth. The collector current of each device is a half-sine pulse with a short overlap into the other half-cycle. Class AB keeps most of the efficiency of class B while removing its crossover notch, which is why almost all audio power amplifiers use it.
Class C

The Q-point is below cut-off: the base is biased negative (for an npn device), so only the peaks of the input drive the transistor into conduction. The conduction angle is less than 180°, commonly 90° to 150°, and the collector current is a train of narrow pulses. A parallel LC tank tuned to the signal frequency serves as the load; each pulse tops up the circulating tank current and the tank rings at its resonant frequency, producing an almost pure sine wave across it (the flywheel effect). Class C therefore suits single-frequency or narrow-band RF power amplifiers and frequency multipliers (tune the tank to a harmonic), but never audio, where the load is broadband.
Class D (Switching Amplifier)

Class D abandons linear operation altogether: the output transistors, usually MOSFETs, are driven as switches that are either fully on (saturated, near zero voltage) or fully off (zero current), so they dissipate very little power in either state. The input signal is compared with a high-frequency triangle wave to produce a pulse-width-modulated (PWM) square wave whose average value follows the input; the switches reproduce this at full supply amplitude and a low-pass LC filter removes the switching frequency, leaving the amplified signal. Efficiencies above 90 % make class D the choice for portable, battery-powered and high-power audio.
