concepts.text: Identifying the class from a description:
items: Transistor always conducting, output an undistorted replica, hot even at idle: class A.
Two transistors each handling one half-cycle, zero idle current, notch at the zero crossing: class B.
Two transistors with a small idle current so that both are on near the zero crossing: class AB.
Current in short pulses, tuned LC load, single frequency: class C.
Transistors switching fully on and off, PWM drive, output filter: class D.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Conduction Angle, Output Stages and Power

The conduction angle follows directly from the bias. If a transistor starts to conduct only when the input sine wave V_p sin ωt exceeds some threshold V_on (its V_BE of about 0.7 V, plus any reverse bias V_BB applied to the base), it conducts between the angles where V_p sin ωt = V_on. That interval is 180° − 2 arcsin(V_on/V_p), which is the same as 2 arccos(V_on/V_p). With V_on = 0 the angle is exactly 180° (ideal class B); with a reverse bias it is less than 180° (class C); and with a forward pre-bias the threshold becomes negative and the angle exceeds 180° (class AB).

concepts.plainText: θc = 2 arccos(V_on / V_p), V_on = input level at which conduction starts

concepts.text: The simplest output stage is a class A emitter follower biased by a constant current source I from the negative rail. Its output can rise to nearly +V_CC, but it can fall only to −I R_L, because at that point the whole bias current flows in the load and the transistor cuts off. Choosing I = V_CC/R_L gives a symmetrical swing of ±V_CC, and the efficiency is then η = (1/4)(V_m/IR_L)(V_m/V_CC), which peaks at 25 %. With no signal the follower still dissipates V_CC × I, so it runs hottest at idle.

In a complementary class B stage with supplies ±V_CC, each supply delivers half-sine current pulses of peak I_m = V_m/R_L, whose average is I_m/π. The total supply power is therefore 2V_CC V_m/(π R_L), while the load receives V_m²/(2R_L). Whatever is left is heat shared equally by the two transistors, and it is greatest not at full output but at V_m = 2V_CC/π.

concepts.latex: P_L = \frac{V_m^2}{2R_L}, \quad P_S = \frac{2V_{CC}V_m}{\pi R_L}, \quad P_D = P_S - P_L
concepts.plainText: PL = Vm²/(2RL); PS = 2 VCC Vm/(π RL); PD = PS − PL (class B, ±VCC)

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: complementary class B, VCC = +/-18 V, RL = 8 ohm, Vm = 15 V
Im = 15/8 = 1.875 A
PL = 15^2/(2 x 8) = 14.06 W
PS = 2 x 18 x 1.875/pi = 21.49 W
eta = 14.06/21.49 = 65.4 %   (check: (pi/4)(15/18) = 65.4 %)
PD (both) = 21.49 - 14.06 = 7.42 W, i.e. 3.71 W per transistor
Worst case per transistor = 18^2/(pi^2 x 8) = 4.10 W at Vm = 2 x 18/pi = 11.46 V

Worked example 2: class A emitter follower, VCC = +/-12 V, RL = 60 ohm, I = 0.2 A
Negative swing limit = -I RL = -12 V, so a 10 V peak output is undistorted
PL = 10^2/(2 x 60) = 0.833 W
PS = 2 VCC I = 2 x 12 x 0.2 = 4.8 W (constant, signal or not)
eta = 0.833/4.8 = 17.4 %   (check: (1/4)(10/12)(10/12) = 17.4 %)
Idle dissipation of the follower = VCC x I = 12 x 0.2 = 2.4 W

Crossover distortion is easy to quantify. In an unbiased complementary pair the output stays at zero while |v_in| is below V_BE(on), so the output peak is V_p − 0.7 V and each transistor conducts for 2 arccos(0.7/V_p). With a 1.4 V peak input that is only 120° per device, leaving a dead zone of 60° around every zero crossing. For class D the losses are of a different kind: a MOSFET with on-resistance R_on in series with the load wastes I²R_on while on, so conduction efficiency is R_L/(R_L + R_on), and every transition adds a switching loss that grows with the switching frequency.

Common slips: using V_m²/R_L instead of V_m²/(2R_L) for load power (peak versus rms); treating the class B supply current as I_m instead of 2I_m/π; assuming class B dissipation is greatest at full output; and forgetting that a class A stage dissipates most with no signal at all.

Two numbers to remember: class B efficiency is proportional to V_m (halve the swing, halve η), while class A efficiency is proportional to V_m² (halve the swing, quarter η). Each class B transistor must be rated for about 0.2 × the maximum output power.

formulas.plainText: Class A Q-point: VCEQ ≈ VCC/2, ICQ ≈ VCC/(2 RL)
Class B push-pull supply current: Idc = 2 Im/π ≈ 0.637 Im
Class D: V_o(avg) = D × VCC, duty cycle D = t_on / T

notes.text: Class is decided only by where the Q-point sits on the load line (centre, at cut-off, just above it, or below it), not by the device or the coupling. When a question describes the Q-point, translate it into a class at once.

In class C the collector current is a pulse but the voltage across the tuned tank is a sine wave. A question about the output waveform of class C expects the sinusoidal tank voltage; a question about the collector current expects pulses.

Class D is not named for digital; it is simply the next letter after C. Its transistors are switches, so the idea of a conduction angle does not really apply, and the output filter, not the transistor, shapes the waveform.

formulas.title: DC load line
formulas.description: Locus of all (V_CE, I_C) operating points for supply V_CC and load R_L; it meets the axes at V_CE = V_CC and I_C = V_CC/R_L.

formulas.title: Class A Q-point (series-fed)
formulas.description: Centre of the load line, giving the largest symmetrical swing; I_CQ flows continuously even with no signal.

formulas.title: Class B supply current
formulas.description: Average current drawn from the supply by a class B push-pull pair when the peak load current is I_m; it is zero with no signal.

formulas.title: Class D average output
formulas.plainText: V_o(avg) = D × VCC, D = t_on / T
formulas.description: Average of the PWM output of a single-supply switching stage; the duty cycle D follows the input signal and the LC filter extracts this average.

flashcards.front: Where is the Q-point for class A, class B and class C operation?
flashcards.back: A: at the centre of the load line. B: at cut-off (I_CQ = 0). C: below cut-off, so the device conducts only on the input peaks.

flashcards.front: Describe the collector-current waveform of one transistor in a class B push-pull stage.
flashcards.back: Half-sine pulses of one polarity lasting 180° of each cycle; the other transistor supplies the opposite half-cycles.

flashcards.front: How does a class C amplifier produce a sinusoidal output from pulses of collector current?
flashcards.back: The load is a parallel LC tank tuned to the signal frequency; each current pulse sustains the tank's oscillation (flywheel effect), giving a sine voltage across it.

questions.questionText: In a class C amplifier the collector current flows in short pulses, yet the output voltage is nearly sinusoidal because:
options: The load is an LC tank tuned to the signal frequency, which rings between pulses
The transistor is biased at the centre of the load line
Two transistors are used in push-pull
questions.explanation: The tuned tank stores energy and oscillates at its resonant frequency; each current pulse merely replaces the energy lost, so the tank voltage is a sine wave (flywheel effect).

questions.questionText: The Q-point of each transistor in a class B push-pull stage is located:
options: At the centre of the DC load line
Slightly above cut-off with a small quiescent current
At cut-off, with essentially zero quiescent collector current
questions.explanation: Class B biases each device at cut-off so it conducts only for the half-cycle that drives it on; the centre of the load line is class A and slightly above cut-off is class AB.

questions.questionText: The conduction angle of each output transistor in a class AB stage is:
questions.explanation: Class AB is biased slightly above cut-off, so each device conducts for a little more than half a cycle but less than the full cycle.

questions.questionText: An amplifier whose transistor conducts for only 120° of each input cycle is operating in:
questions.explanation: A conduction angle below 180° defines class C; class B is exactly 180°, class AB between 180° and 360°, and class A the full 360°.

questions.questionText: A transistor in a power stage conducts for 270° of each input cycle. Its class of operation is:
questions.explanation: 270° lies between 180° and 360°, which is class AB.

questions.questionText: In a class C amplifier the base of an npn transistor is biased:
options: At the centre of the DC load line
Below cut-off, with a reverse (negative) DC bias, so only the input peaks cause conduction
Exactly at cut-off with zero base bias
Slightly above cut-off with a small forward bias
questions.explanation: Class C places the Q-point beyond cut-off, so the input must first overcome the reverse bias and V_BE before any collector current flows, giving conduction for less than 180°.

questions.questionText: The low-pass LC filter at the output of a class D amplifier is needed to:
options: Remove the high-frequency switching component and leave the amplified audio signal
Generate the triangle carrier for the modulator
Bias the MOSFETs at the edge of conduction
Store energy between current pulses at the signal frequency, as in a class C tank
questions.explanation: The switches produce a full-amplitude PWM square wave; the filter passes its slowly varying average (the audio) and rejects the switching frequency and its harmonics.

questions.questionText: Crossover distortion in an unbiased complementary class B stage is caused by:
options: Both transistors conducting simultaneously near the zero crossing
Saturation of the transistors at the signal peaks
Neither transistor conducting while the input is below about ±0.7 V
The output coupling capacitor blocking low frequencies
questions.explanation: Each base-emitter junction needs about 0.7 V to turn on, so for small input levels around zero both transistors are off and the output stays at zero, producing a step at each crossing.

questions.questionText: An unbiased complementary class B emitter-follower stage uses silicon transistors (V_BE(on) = 0.7 V). The input is a sine wave of 5 V peak. Ignoring other losses, the peak output voltage is:
questions.explanation: The output follows the input minus one V_BE drop: 5 − 0.7 = 4.3 V. Subtracting 2V_BE (3.6 V) confuses it with the voltage between the two bases.

questions.questionText: An unbiased complementary class B stage has V_BE(on) = 0.7 V for each transistor and is driven by a 1.4 V peak sine wave. For how many degrees of each cycle does each transistor conduct?
questions.explanation: Conduction starts when 1.4 sin θ = 0.7, i.e. θ = 30°, and ends at 150°, so each device conducts for 150° − 30° = 120° instead of the ideal 180°.

questions.questionText: An emitter follower is widely used as a power output stage mainly because it:
options: Conducts for less than 180° and is therefore very efficient
Inverts the signal, cancelling even harmonics
Has a low output resistance and so can drive a low-resistance load without losing gain
questions.explanation: The follower's output resistance is only about r_e plus the source resistance divided by β, so a loudspeaker of a few ohms receives almost the full voltage; its voltage gain is just below 1.

questions.questionText: A class A emitter-follower output stage runs from ±12 V, drives R_L = 100 Ω and is biased by a 120 mA constant current source. Ignoring saturation voltages, its efficiency at the largest undistorted output is:
A series-fed class A amplifier with V_CC = 20 V and a collector load of 20 Ω is biased at the centre of its load line. The maximum AC power it can deliver to the load is:
questions.explanation: Peak voltage = V_CC/2 = 10 V and peak current = I_CQ = 0.5 A, so P_ac = (10 × 0.5)/2 = 2.5 W, i.e. V_CC²/(8R_L). The 10 W figure is the DC input power.

questions.questionText: A series-fed class A stage with V_CC = 24 V and R_C = 24 Ω is biased at I_CQ = 0.5 A. A signal produces a sinusoidal collector current of 0.3 A peak. Its efficiency is:
questions.explanation: P_ac = I_p² R_C/2 = 0.09 × 24/2 = 1.08 W; P_dc = V_CC I_CQ = 12 W; η = 1.08/12 = 9 %. Forgetting the 1/2 of the rms conversion gives 18 %.

questions.questionText: A transformer-coupled class A amplifier operates from V_CC = 12 V with a quiescent collector current of 250 mA. The maximum AC power it can deliver to the load (ideal transformer) is:
questions.explanation: P_dc = 12 × 0.25 = 3 W, and the theoretical maximum efficiency of transformer-coupled class A is 50 %, so P_ac(max) = 1.5 W. The 0.75 W figure uses the 25 % series-fed limit.

questions.questionText: In a transformer-coupled class A amplifier with V_CC = 10 V, the collector voltage swings between 4 V and 16 V. Using η = 50 % × [(V_max − V_min)/(V_max + V_min)]², its efficiency is:
A class B push-pull stage with V_CC = 20 V delivers a sine output of 10 V peak. Its efficiency is approximately:
questions.explanation: η = (π/4)(V_m/V_CC) = 0.785 × 10/20 = 39.3 %. The 78.5 % limit applies only at full swing V_m = V_CC.

questions.questionText: A complementary class B stage runs from ±15 V and drives an 8 Ω load with an output of 12 V peak. The total DC power drawn from the two supplies is approximately:
questions.explanation: I_m = 12/8 = 1.5 A; each supply provides an average of I_m/π, so P_S = 2V_CC I_m/π = 2 × 15 × 1.5/π = 14.3 W. The 9 W figure is the load power.

questions.questionText: A complementary class B stage with supplies of ±20 V drives an 8 Ω load with 16 V peak output. The power dissipated in each output transistor is approximately:
questions.explanation: I_m = 2 A; P_S = 2 × 20 × 2/π = 25.46 W; P_L = 16²/(2 × 8) = 16 W; P_D = 9.46 W for the pair, so 4.73 W per transistor.

questions.questionText: A complementary class B amplifier uses ±12 V supplies and an 8 Ω load. The maximum power that each transistor may have to dissipate, over all signal levels, is approximately:
questions.explanation: Worst-case dissipation occurs at V_m = 2V_CC/π and totals 2V_CC²/(π²R_L) = 2 × 144/(9.87 × 8) = 3.65 W, which is 1.82 W per transistor.

questions.questionText: Ignoring saturation voltages, the maximum sine-wave power a complementary class B stage with ±15 V supplies can deliver into an 8 Ω load is:
questions.explanation: At full swing V_m = V_CC = 15 V: P_L = V_m²/(2R_L) = 225/16 = 14.1 W. Using V_m²/R_L gives 28.1 W.

questions.questionText: A class B complementary stage is designed for a maximum sine output of 20 W. The worst-case dissipation for which each output transistor must be rated is approximately:
questions.explanation: Per-transistor worst case V_CC²/(π²R_L) divided by P_L(max) = V_CC²/(2R_L) is 2/π² = 0.203, so each device needs about 0.203 × 20 = 4.05 W; 8.1 W is for the pair.

questions.questionText: In a class B push-pull stage with V_CC = 18 V, the transistor dissipation is greatest when the peak output voltage is approximately:
questions.explanation: Dissipation peaks at V_m = 2V_CC/π = 36/π = 11.5 V, not at full output.

questions.questionText: A series-fed class A stage has V_CC = 12 V, R_C = 6 Ω and a quiescent current of 1 A. With no input signal, the power dissipated in the transistor is:
questions.explanation: V_CEQ = 12 − 1 × 6 = 6 V, so P_D = V_CEQ × I_CQ = 6 W. The supply delivers 12 W, of which the other 6 W heats R_C.

questions.questionText: In a class A power amplifier, the power dissipated in the transistor is greatest when:
options: The output is at its maximum undistorted swing
The output swing is 63.7 % of V_CC
The load is open-circuited during full swing
questions.explanation: The DC input power of class A is constant; P_D = P_dc − P_ac, so the transistor dissipates most when P_ac = 0, i.e. at idle.

questions.questionText: Which statement about power dissipation in a class B push-pull stage is correct?
options: It is greatest with no signal, as in class A
It rises continuously and is greatest at full output swing
It is independent of the signal level
It is zero with no signal and reaches its maximum at a peak output of about 0.64 V_CC
questions.explanation: With zero quiescent current there is no idle loss; P_D = P_S − P_L rises and then falls with swing, peaking at V_m = 2V_CC/π ≈ 0.637 V_CC.

questions.questionText: A class AB complementary output stage runs from ±15 V and is biased at a quiescent current of 20 mA. The power drawn from the supplies with no signal is:
questions.explanation: The quiescent current flows from +15 V through both transistors to −15 V, a total of 30 V: P = 30 × 0.02 = 0.6 W. Zero would be true only for pure class B.

questions.questionText: The output of an unbiased class B stage driven by a small sine wave shows a flat step each time the waveform passes through zero. This defect is called:
questions.explanation: The flat step around the zero crossing, where neither transistor conducts, is crossover distortion; clipping occurs at the peaks.

questions.questionText: A class C amplifier is driven at 10 MHz and its collector tank is tuned to 30 MHz. The output frequency is:
questions.explanation: The pulsed collector current is rich in harmonics; a tank tuned to the third harmonic selects 3 × 10 = 30 MHz, so the stage acts as a frequency tripler.

questions.questionText: In a class C stage the transistor begins to conduct only when the input exceeds 2.0 V (reverse bias plus V_BE). If the input is a sine wave of 2.83 V peak, the conduction angle is approximately:
questions.explanation: Conduction begins where 2.83 sin θ = 2.0, i.e. θ ≈ 45°, and ends at 135°, so θ_c = 135° − 45° = 90° (equivalently 2 arccos(2.0/2.83)).

questions.questionText: A class C stage cannot be used as a wide-band audio amplifier because:
options: Its efficiency is too low for audio power levels
It requires a complementary npn-pnp pair
Its collector current is a train of narrow pulses, and a sine output is restored only by a load tuned to one frequency
questions.explanation: Without a tuned tank the output would be the distorted pulse train itself; the tank works at a single frequency, which is unsuitable for a broadband audio signal.

questions.questionText: A class D half-bridge switches its output between 0 V and 24 V. When the duty cycle is 0.6, the average (filtered) output voltage is:
questions.explanation: V_o(avg) = D × V_DD = 0.6 × 24 = 14.4 V; 9.6 V would be the result of using the off-time fraction.

questions.questionText: In a class D stage only one MOSFET conducts at a time, each having an on-resistance of 0.1 Ω, and the load is 8 Ω. Neglecting switching and filter losses, the efficiency is approximately:
questions.explanation: The on-switch is in series with the load, so η = R_L/(R_L + R_on) = 8/8.1 = 98.8 %. 1.2 % is the fraction lost, not the efficiency.

questions.questionText: In a class D amplifier the pulse-width-modulated drive signal is usually generated by:
options: Passing the input through a tuned LC tank
Comparing the input signal with a high-frequency triangle wave in a comparator
Rectifying the input with a bridge rectifier
Biasing the output transistors slightly above cut-off
questions.explanation: The comparator output is high whenever the input exceeds the triangle, so the pulse width follows the instantaneous input level.

questions.questionText: The output transistors of a class D amplifier dissipate very little power because:
options: When on their voltage is almost zero and when off their current is almost zero, so the V × I product stays small
They conduct for exactly 180° of each cycle
Their quiescent current is set just above cut-off
The output filter absorbs the heat
questions.explanation: Dissipation is the product of device voltage and current; a switch that is fully on or fully off keeps one of them near zero except during the brief transitions.

questions.questionText: A class D audio amplifier must reproduce signals up to 20 kHz. Which switching frequency is the most suitable?
questions.explanation: The switching frequency must be many times the highest audio frequency so the output filter can remove it without affecting the audio band; 400 kHz is 20 times 20 kHz.

questions.questionText: In a complementary-symmetry class B output stage, during the positive half-cycle of the input:
options: The pnp transistor conducts and the npn transistor is cut off
The npn transistor conducts and the pnp transistor is cut off
questions.explanation: A positive input forward-biases the npn base-emitter junction and reverse-biases the pnp one, so the npn device sources current into the load; the roles reverse on the negative half-cycle.

questions.questionText: Which statement about a complementary-symmetry push-pull output stage is correct?
options: It requires both transistors to be of the same polarity (both npn)
It needs a phase-splitter to produce two antiphase drive signals
It needs no centre-tapped transformer, because the joined emitters of the npn and pnp devices drive the load directly
It cannot be operated from a single supply
questions.explanation: The opposite polarities of the npn and pnp devices mean one input signal turns on one device per half-cycle, so no phase splitter or transformer is needed; a single supply with an output capacitor also works.

questions.questionText: A complementary class B stage is powered from a single 24 V supply, with the midpoint coupled to an 8 Ω load through a large capacitor. Ignoring saturation voltages, the maximum sine output power is:
questions.explanation: The midpoint sits at 12 V, so the peak swing is V_CC/2 = 12 V and P = 12²/(2 × 8) = 9 W. Using the full 24 V gives 36 W.

questions.questionText: A complementary class B amplifier must deliver 25 W of sine power into an 8 Ω load. If each transistor has V_CE(sat) = 2 V, the minimum symmetrical supply voltage is:
questions.explanation: V_m = √(2 P R_L) = √(2 × 25 × 8) = 20 V peak; allowing 2 V saturation, V_CC = 20 + 2 = 22 V on each rail. 14.1 V is the rms output.

questions.questionText: In a transformer-coupled class B push-pull amplifier each transistor carries half-sine pulses of 3 A peak. The average current drawn from the single supply is approximately:
questions.explanation: Each transistor averages I_m/π = 0.955 A and both draw from the same supply, so I_dc = 2I_m/π = 1.91 A. 2.12 A is the rms value of a 3 A sine.

questions.questionText: In a class B push-pull stage, reducing the peak output voltage to half its previous value changes the efficiency to:
options: One quarter of its previous value
questions.explanation: η = (π/4)(V_m/V_CC) is directly proportional to V_m, so halving the swing halves the efficiency. In class A, where η is proportional to V_m², it would fall to one quarter.

questions.questionText: A series-fed class A amplifier with V_CC = 24 V is biased at the centre of its load line. When the peak output voltage is 6 V, its efficiency is:
questions.explanation: At centre bias P_dc = V_CC²/(2R_C) and P_ac = V_m²/(2R_C), so η = (V_m/V_CC)² = (6/24)² = 6.25 %. Class A efficiency falls with the square of the swing.

questions.questionText: A series-fed (resistive-load) class A stage is limited to 25 % efficiency, whereas a transformer-coupled one can reach 50 %, because:
options: The transformer-coupled stage conducts for only 180°
The transformer adds energy to the signal
The series-fed stage has a higher quiescent current for the same load
In the series-fed stage the DC collector current also flows in the load resistor, wasting power and limiting the swing to V_CC/2
questions.explanation: With a transformer the load carries no DC and the collector can swing from nearly 0 to 2V_CC, doubling the AC output for the same DC input power.

questions.questionText: The theoretical maximum efficiency π/4 of a class B push-pull stage is reached when:
options: The peak output voltage equals the supply voltage V_CC
The quiescent current is set at a few milliamperes
questions.explanation: η = (π/4)(V_m/V_CC) reaches its maximum of 78.5 % only when V_m = V_CC; at 2V_CC/π the transistor dissipation is maximum instead.

questions.questionText: Which statement about output-stage classes is NOT correct?
options: A class A transistor conducts for the whole cycle
Each class B transistor conducts for half of each cycle
A class C transistor conducts for more than 180° of each cycle
Class D output transistors operate as switches
questions.explanation: Class C conducts for less than 180°, which is why it needs a tuned load; the other three statements are the standard definitions.

questions.questionText: A class A emitter-follower output stage uses ±15 V supplies, a 0.2 A constant current source as its emitter bias, and a 50 Ω load. Ignoring saturation voltages, the largest symmetrical (undistorted) peak output voltage is:
questions.explanation: The output can rise to about +15 V but can fall only to −I R_L = −0.2 × 50 = −10 V before the transistor cuts off, so the symmetrical limit is 10 V peak.

questions.questionText: A class A emitter-follower output stage with ±15 V supplies, 0.2 A constant-current emitter bias and a 50 Ω load delivers a 10 V peak sine output. Its efficiency is approximately:
questions.explanation: P_L = 10²/(2 × 50) = 1 W; the supplies deliver 2 × 15 × 0.2 = 6 W regardless of signal; η = 1/6 = 16.7 %. Counting only one supply gives 33.3 %.

subtopics.title: Comparison of Amplifier Classes
subtopics.subtitle: Efficiency derivations, distortion, heat sinking, cost and choosing the right class

concepts.text: Efficiency of Class A

In a series-fed (RC-coupled) class A stage the Q-point sits at the centre of the load line, so V_CEQ = V_CC/2 and the supply delivers a steady P_dc = V_CC × I_CQ whatever the signal. The largest undistorted output has peak voltage V_CC/2 and peak current I_CQ, giving an AC load power P_ac = (V_CC/2)(I_CQ)/2 = V_CC I_CQ/4, so the maximum efficiency is 25 % and at smaller signals it is lower still. With a transformer-coupled load there is no DC voltage drop across the load, so the collector can swing over the full V_CC (peak voltage V_CC, peak current I_CQ): P_ac = V_CC I_CQ/2 and the maximum efficiency doubles to 50 %.

concepts.plainText: η_A (series-fed) = (VCC·ICQ/4) / (VCC·ICQ) = 25 %
η_A (transformer coupled) = (VCC·ICQ/2) / (VCC·ICQ) = 50 %

concepts.text: Efficiency of Classes B, AB, C and D

In a class B push-pull stage each transistor draws half-sine pulses of peak I_m, whose average is I_m/π; the two together draw I_dc = 2I_m/π from the supply, so P_dc = 2V_CC I_m/π. The load receives P_ac = V_m I_m/2, where V_m is the peak output voltage. Dividing gives η = (π/4)(V_m/V_CC), which reaches its maximum of π/4 = 78.5 % when the output swings the full supply voltage (V_m = V_CC) and falls in proportion to V_m at lower volume. Class AB lies between 50 % and 78.5 % because its small quiescent current adds to P_dc. Class C reaches about 90 % because current flows only while the collector voltage is near its minimum, and class D exceeds 90 % because a switch that is either fully on or fully off dissipates almost nothing.
Distortion, Linearity and Heat

Class A has the best linearity: the transistor never leaves the active region and never switches, so harmonic distortion is lowest. Class B adds crossover distortion where one transistor hands over to the other; class AB removes that notch and approaches class A quality. Class C is grossly non-linear (its current is a pulse) and is acceptable only because a tuned load discards the harmonics, while class D linearity depends on the accuracy of the PWM modulator and the quality of the output filter, and switching noise must be kept out of the load. Distortion is quantified as total harmonic distortion (THD).

Heat is the practical penalty of low efficiency. A class A stage dissipates its maximum power, P_D = V_CC I_CQ, with no signal at all, so its heat sink must handle the full quiescent loss and the transistor actually runs cooler when a signal is present. A class B stage dissipates nothing at idle; its worst case is not at full output but when the peak swing is 2V_CC/π, about 0.637 V_CC, where the two transistors together dissipate 2V_CC²/(π²R_L), roughly 40 % of the maximum output power (one fifth per transistor). In complexity and cost, class A is simplest (one transistor, but a large heat sink or an output transformer), class B and AB need two matched transistors plus a bias network, and class D needs a modulator, gate drivers and an LC filter yet gets away with the smallest heat sink.

concepts.plainText: Class B: P_D(max, both devices) = 2 VCC² / (π² RL) at Vm = 2 VCC/π

concepts.text: Push-Pull Operation and Crossover Distortion

In a push-pull stage two matched transistors are driven by signals of opposite phase, obtained from a centre-tapped input transformer or a phase splitter, or simply by using a complementary npn-pnp pair fed from the same point; each transistor supplies one half-cycle and the outputs combine in the load. Because the two devices are driven in antiphase, the even harmonics (2nd, 4th and so on) that each generates through its own non-linearity are equal and opposite and cancel in the output, while the fundamental and the odd harmonics add, so the dominant residual distortion is the 3rd harmonic. In a transformer-coupled version the DC components also cancel, so the core does not saturate, and supply ripple appearing in both halves is cancelled too. The result is more output power, higher efficiency and lower distortion than a single-ended stage built from the same devices.

Crossover distortion arises in a pure class B pair because each base-emitter junction needs about 0.7 V before it conducts. While the input lies between roughly −0.7 V and +0.7 V neither transistor is on, so the output stays at zero and the sine wave acquires a flat step at every zero crossing. The step is of fixed size, so the relative distortion is worst for small signals, and it is rich in odd harmonics that sound harsh. The cure is to bias each base to the edge of conduction (class AB) with a small forward voltage supplied by diodes or a V_BE multiplier; negative feedback around the stage reduces the residual further.

rows: Small-signal and preamplifier stages, low-power hi-fi, RF driver stages
Crossover distortion at the zero crossing
Push-pull power stages where idle power must be zero
Very low once biased just above cut-off
Audio power amplifiers, hi-fi, public address, op-amp output stages
Very high; usable only with a tuned load
RF transmitter power amplifiers, frequency multipliers
Low after LC filtering; some switching noise
Portable and battery audio, subwoofer and car amplifiers

concepts.text: Choosing a class:
items: Audio (hi-fi, public address): class AB. It removes crossover distortion at little cost in efficiency; class A only where the lowest possible distortion outweighs heat and power consumption.
RF at a single frequency (transmitters, frequency multipliers): class C with a tuned tank for maximum efficiency; class A or AB where a modulated RF signal must be amplified linearly.
Battery-powered and compact equipment: class D, because efficiency above 90 % means longer battery life and little heat sinking; class AB when the simplest low-noise design is preferred.
Small-signal voltage amplification anywhere: class A, because efficiency is irrelevant at milliwatt levels and linearity is paramount.

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Comparing and Choosing Classes

Efficiency tells how much supply power reaches the load, but the number that fixes the size and cost of the output transistors is the figure of merit: the largest power a device must dissipate divided by the largest power the stage can deliver to the load. A transformer-coupled class A stage dissipates its whole quiescent input V_CC I_CQ with no signal, while its maximum load power is only half of that, so its figure of merit is 2: a 10 W class A amplifier needs a transistor able to dissipate 20 W. In a class B pair each transistor's worst-case dissipation is V_CC²/(π²R_L) against a maximum load power of V_CC²/(2R_L), a ratio of 2/π², about 0.2. The same transistor can therefore deliver roughly ten times more power in class B than in class A.

concepts.plainText: Figure of merit = P_D(max)/P_L(max): class A (transformer coupled) = 2; class B = 2/π² ≈ 0.2 per transistor

concepts.text: Maximum efficiency is quoted at full output, yet speech and music spend most of the time far below full output. In a transformer-coupled class A stage the supply power is constant, so efficiency is directly proportional to the output power: at one tenth of full power it is only 5 %. In class B the supply current follows the signal amplitude, so efficiency falls only with the square root of the output power and is still about 25 % at one tenth of full power. This is why class B and AB stages run cool at normal listening levels while a class A stage runs hot all the time.

Reducing the conduction angle raises the ideal efficiency because current then flows only while the voltage across the transistor is near its minimum. For an ideal stage whose output swings the full supply, the efficiency depends on the conduction angle θ (in radians) as shown below; it gives 50 % at 360° and 78.5 % at 180°, the class A and class B limits, then about 84 % at 150°, 90 % at 120° and 94 % at 90°, approaching 100 % as θ shrinks. The price is that the fundamental output power for a given peak current falls, so practical class C stages settle at 120° to 150°. Class D escapes this trade-off by switching: its losses come from the on-resistance of the switches (conduction loss), the finite rise and fall times (switching loss, proportional to switching frequency), gate drive and the output filter.

concepts.plainText: η = (θ − sin θ) / (4[sin(θ/2) − (θ/2)cos(θ/2)])  (ideal, full swing, θ = conduction angle in rad)

concepts.text:
Worked example 1: 20 W into the load at full output
Class A (transformer, 50 %): P_dc = 20/0.5 = 40 W, taken all the time
  Transistor heat: 40 W at idle, 20 W at full output -> rating >= 40 W
Class B (78.5 %): P_dc = 20/0.785 = 25.5 W
  Heat at full output = 25.5 - 20 = 5.5 W (both devices)
  Worst case = 0.405 x 20 = 8.1 W total, about 4 W per transistor
Class D (90 %): P_dc = 20/0.9 = 22.2 W, heat = 2.2 W
Conclusion: A needs a 40 W device and a large heat sink;
  B needs two 4 W devices; D needs the smallest heat sink.

Worked example 2: battery life, 12 V 5 Ah battery (60 Wh usable)
Average output 10 W
Class AB at 60 %: P_in = 10/0.60 = 16.7 W -> 60/16.7 = 3.6 h
Class D at 90 %:  P_in = 10/0.90 = 11.1 W -> 60/11.1 = 5.4 h
Switching to class D gives 50 % more playing time
  and cuts the heat from 6.7 W to 1.1 W.
Common mistakes when comparing classes:
items: Quoting the maximum efficiency for a stage that is running below full output; efficiency must be scaled for the actual level.
Sizing a class A transistor for the output power; it must be rated for the full quiescent dissipation, twice the maximum output.
Assuming class B dissipation is greatest at full output; it peaks at about 40 % of maximum output power.
Choosing class C for any wideband signal such as audio or an amplitude-modulated signal that must be amplified linearly.
Treating class D as distortion-free; its linearity depends on the modulator, dead time and output filter, and its fast edges cause electromagnetic interference.

concepts.text: For a selection question, ask three things in order: is the signal wideband (rules out class C), is lowest distortion at low power the aim (class A), and is efficiency or battery life the priority (class D, otherwise class AB).

formulas.plainText: Class B: P_dc = 2 VCC Im/π; P_ac = Vm Im/2
P_D(max, class B pair) = 2 VCC² / (π² RL) at Vm = 2 VCC/π

notes.text: Three efficiency numbers to memorise: 25 % (class A, series-fed or resistive load), 50 % (class A, transformer coupled) and 78.5 % (class B, equal to π/4). If a question specifies a resistive or RC-coupled load, answer 25 %; an unqualified 'maximum efficiency of a class A amplifier' question usually expects 50 %, the transformer-coupled figure.
Class A runs hottest with no signal; class B dissipates most at about 64 % of full swing, not at maximum output. A heat-sink question for class A must use the quiescent power V_CC I_CQ.

Push-pull cancels even harmonics and DC in the transformer core, but it does not cancel odd harmonics and does not by itself remove crossover distortion, which is an odd-harmonic effect cured by class AB bias.
π/4 = 0.785. For class B at less than full swing, scale the efficiency: at half the maximum swing it is 78.5 % × 0.5 = 39.3 %.

formulas.title: Class A efficiency, series-fed
formulas.description: Resistive (RC-coupled) load with Q at the centre of the load line: peak swing V_CC/2 and I_CQ, constant P_dc = V_CC I_CQ.

formulas.title: Class A efficiency, transformer coupled
formulas.description: No DC drop across the load, so the collector swings the full V_CC and the AC power doubles for the same DC input.

formulas.title: Class B efficiency
formulas.description: V_m is the peak output voltage of a push-pull pair fed from V_CC; the maximum occurs when V_m = V_CC.

formulas.title: Transistor dissipation
formulas.description: Power turned into heat in the output device(s); for class A with no signal P_D = V_CC I_CQ, its maximum.

formulas.title: Class B maximum dissipation
formulas.plainText: P_D(max) = 2 VCC² / (π² RL) at Vm = 2 VCC/π
formulas.description: Worst-case total dissipation of a class B push-pull pair (half in each transistor), occurring at 63.7 % of full swing and equal to about 0.4 of the maximum load power.

flashcards.front: Why is the maximum efficiency of a transformer-coupled class A stage twice that of a series-fed one?
flashcards.back: No DC voltage is dropped across the load, so the collector swings over the full V_CC instead of V_CC/2, doubling P_ac for the same P_dc: 50 % instead of 25 %.

flashcards.front: Derive the maximum efficiency of a class B push-pull amplifier in one line.
flashcards.back: P_dc = 2V_CC I_m/π and P_ac = V_m I_m/2, so η = (π/4)(V_m/V_CC); the maximum is π/4 = 78.5 % at V_m = V_CC.

flashcards.front: Which harmonics cancel in a push-pull stage, and why?
flashcards.back: Even harmonics (2nd, 4th, ...) cancel because the two antiphase-driven transistors produce them in phase opposition at the output; odd harmonics add.

flashcards.front: At what output level does a class B stage dissipate the most heat?
flashcards.back: At a peak swing of 2V_CC/π, about 0.637 V_CC, not at full output; total P_D = 2V_CC²/(π² R_L). At idle it dissipates nothing.

questions.questionText: Classes A, B and C arranged in increasing order of conduction angle are:
options: Class C, class B, class A
Class A, class B, class C
Class B, class C, class A
Class C, class A, class B
questions.explanation: Class C conducts for less than 180°, class B for 180° and class A for the full 360°.

questions.questionText: Which class of amplifier draws the same average current from the supply whether or not a signal is present?
questions.explanation: In class A the transistor is biased at the centre of the load line, so the supply delivers a steady V_CC I_CQ at all signal levels. Classes B, C and D draw current that rises with the signal.

questions.questionText: Which ordering of the maximum theoretical efficiency is correct?
options: Class B < class A < class C
Class C < class B < class A
Class A < class B < class C
Class A < class C < class B
questions.explanation: Efficiency rises as the conduction angle falls: class A at most 50 %, class B 78.5 %, class C about 90 % or more.

questions.questionText: The figure of merit P_D(max)/P_L(max) of a power amplifier compares:
options: The output power with the power taken from the supply
The load power with the input signal power
The peak collector current with the quiescent collector current
The largest power the output transistor must dissipate with the largest power delivered to the load
questions.explanation: The figure of merit sets the transistor dissipation rating needed for a given output; output/supply power is the efficiency and load/input power is the power gain.

questions.questionText: A transistor rated for 20 W maximum dissipation is used in an ideal transformer-coupled class A amplifier. The largest output power it can deliver without exceeding its rating is:
questions.explanation: The figure of merit of transformer-coupled class A is 2: P_D(max) = V_CC I_CQ at idle and P_L(max) = V_CC I_CQ/2, so P_L(max) = 20/2 = 10 W.

questions.questionText: In an ideal class B push-pull amplifier, the maximum dissipation of EACH transistor, as a fraction of the maximum load power, is about:
questions.explanation: Each transistor dissipates at most V_CC²/(π²R_L) while P_L(max) = V_CC²/(2R_L); the ratio is 2/π² = 0.203. The 0.4 figure is for both transistors together.

questions.questionText: An ideal class B push-pull stage must deliver a maximum of 25 W to its load. The minimum dissipation rating needed for each output transistor is about:
questions.explanation: Each device dissipates at most (2/π²)P_L(max) = 0.203 × 25 = 5.07 W. 10 W is the total for both devices and 50 W would be needed by a class A stage.

questions.questionText: Power transistors rated for 15 W dissipation each are available. Ideally, what maximum output power can one of them give as a transformer-coupled class A stage, and two of them as a class B push-pull pair?
options: 30 W in class A and about 37 W in class B
7.5 W in class A and about 74 W in class B
7.5 W in class A and about 37 W in class B
15 W in class A and about 74 W in class B
questions.explanation: Class A: P_L(max) = P_D(max)/2 = 7.5 W. Class B: each device dissipates at most 0.203 P_L(max), so P_L(max) = 15/0.203 = 74 W.

questions.questionText: A transformer-coupled class A amplifier runs from V_CC = 12 V with I_CQ = 0.5 A. Assuming ideal operation, the transistor dissipation with no signal and at maximum output is:
options: 3 W with no signal and 6 W at maximum output
0 W with no signal and 3 W at maximum output
6 W with no signal and 6 W at maximum output
6 W with no signal and 3 W at maximum output
questions.explanation: P_dc = 12 × 0.5 = 6 W at all times. With no signal all of it is dissipated; at maximum output P_ac = 6/2 = 3 W goes to the load, leaving P_D = 6 − 3 = 3 W.

questions.questionText: Which statement about output-transistor dissipation versus signal level is correct?
options: Both class A and class B dissipate most at full output
Class A dissipation rises with signal while class B dissipation falls with signal
Class A dissipation is greatest with no signal, while class B dissipation is zero with no signal and peaks below full output
Neither class A nor class B dissipates power with no signal
questions.explanation: Class A takes constant supply power, so the more goes to the load the less heats the transistor. Class B dissipates nothing at idle and most at a swing of about 0.637 V_CC.

questions.questionText: A transformer-coupled class A stage and a class B push-pull stage are each operated with their peak output swing reduced to half the maximum possible. Their ideal efficiencies are:
options: 25 % for class A and 39.3 % for class B
12.5 % for class A and 39.3 % for class B
25 % for class A and 78.5 % for class B
12.5 % for class A and 19.6 % for class B

questions.questionText: An ideal class B amplifier is delivering one tenth of its maximum output power. Its efficiency is about:
questions.explanation: Power scales as V_m², so V_m/V_CC = √0.1 = 0.316 and η = 78.5 % × 0.316 = 24.8 %. Scaling by 0.1 directly (7.85 %) is the class A rule, not class B.

questions.questionText: With speech or music, whose average level is far below full output, a class B or AB stage wastes much less power than a class A stage because:
options: Class A draws its full supply power all the time, whereas the class B supply current falls with the signal amplitude
Class B has a higher voltage gain than class A
Class A transistors have a lower current rating
Class B uses an output transformer that stores the unused energy
questions.explanation: The class A supply power V_CC I_CQ is constant, so at low output nearly all of it becomes heat. The class B supply current 2I_m/π is proportional to the signal peak.

questions.questionText: An amplifier must deliver 10 W at full output. Ideally, the power taken from the supply by a transformer-coupled class A stage and by a class B push-pull stage is:
options: 40 W for class A and 12.7 W for class B
12.7 W for class A and 20 W for class B
20 W for class A and 7.85 W for class B
20 W for class A and 12.7 W for class B
questions.explanation: P_dc = P_L/η: class A 10/0.5 = 20 W; class B 10/0.785 = 12.7 W. Multiplying by the efficiency (7.85 W) is the common slip.

questions.questionText: A 100 W audio amplifier can be built as class AB with 70 % efficiency or as class D with 92 % efficiency at full output. The heat to be removed at full output in each case is:
options: 30 W for class AB and 8 W for class D
42.9 W for class AB and 8.7 W for class D
142.9 W for class AB and 108.7 W for class D
70 W for class AB and 92 W for class D
questions.explanation: Heat = P_L/η − P_L: class AB 100/0.70 − 100 = 42.9 W; class D 100/0.92 − 100 = 8.7 W. Taking (1 − η) × P_L gives the wrong 30 W and 8 W.

questions.questionText: A portable speaker has a 12 V, 7.2 Ah battery (assume all 86.4 Wh are usable) and delivers a steady 20 W average output. The playing time with a class AB stage of 60 % efficiency and with a class D stage of 90 % efficiency is:
options: 7.2 h for class AB and 4.8 h for class D
2.59 h for class AB and 3.89 h for class D
3.89 h for class AB and 2.59 h for class D
questions.explanation: Input power = 20/0.6 = 33.3 W and 20/0.9 = 22.2 W; time = 86.4 Wh / 33.3 W = 2.59 h and 86.4/22.2 = 3.89 h. Ignoring efficiency gives 86.4/20 = 4.32 h for both.

questions.questionText: A class D amplifier with 92 % efficiency delivers 46 W to a loudspeaker. The power drawn from the supply and the power lost as heat are:
questions.explanation: P_dc = 46/0.92 = 50 W and the loss is 50 − 46 = 4 W.

questions.questionText: A class D half-bridge delivers 50 W of sine-wave power into 8 Ω. Its MOSFETs each have R_DS(on) = 0.1 Ω and one of them always carries the load current. The conduction loss in the switches is:
questions.explanation: I_rms = √(P/R) = √(50/8) = 2.5 A; conduction loss = I_rms² × R_DS(on) = 6.25 × 0.1 = 0.625 W. Using the peak current gives 1.25 W.

questions.questionText: A 30 W (full-output) amplifier is redesigned from class AB at 65 % efficiency to class D at 90 % efficiency. The reduction in supply power at full output is about:
An audio power amplifier driving a loudspeaker is measured to have 85 % efficiency at full output. Which class is it most likely to be?
questions.explanation: Linear classes cannot exceed the class B limit of 78.5 %, and class C cannot reproduce a wideband audio signal, so an 85 % audio amplifier must be a switching (class D) design.

questions.questionText: An ideal class B push-pull stage dissipates the most heat when its output power is about what fraction of its maximum output power?
questions.explanation: Maximum dissipation occurs at V_m = 2V_CC/π = 0.637 V_CC; power goes as V_m², so P_L/P_L(max) = (2/π)² = 0.405. The 63.7 % figure is the voltage ratio, not the power ratio.

questions.questionText: A class B complementary stage runs from ±20 V into an 8 Ω load. The worst-case dissipation of each transistor is:
questions.explanation: P_D(max) per transistor = V_CC²/(π²R_L) = 400/(9.87 × 8) = 5.07 W; 10.1 W is the total for both, and 25 W is the maximum load power.

questions.questionText: For the same maximum load power of 25 W, a transformer-coupled class A design needs a transistor rated for 50 W, whereas a class B design needs two transistors each rated for about 5.07 W. The ratio of the class A rating to each class B rating is about:
questions.explanation: 50/5.07 = 9.9, about 10, which is the ratio of the figures of merit 2/(2/π²) = π².

questions.questionText: An ideal class B stage at full output (78.5 % efficiency) produces how much heat for every watt delivered to the load?
questions.explanation: Heat per watt = 1/η − 1 = 4/π − 1 = 1.273 − 1 = 0.273 W. The figure 1 − 0.785 = 0.215 W is heat per watt of supply power, not per watt of output.

questions.questionText: Class C amplifiers are not used as audio power amplifiers because:
options: Their efficiency is too low for audio
They need two transistors in push-pull
The collector current is a train of pulses rich in harmonics, and a tuned tank can restore only one frequency, not a whole audio band
They cannot be operated from a DC supply
questions.explanation: A class C stage relies on a resonant tank to rebuild a sine wave at one frequency; a wideband signal such as audio would be severely distorted. Its efficiency is actually the highest of the bias classes A, B, AB and C.

questions.questionText: For the highest efficiency in the final power stage of an FM broadcast transmitter, whose signal has constant amplitude, the preferred class is:
questions.explanation: An FM carrier has a constant envelope and a single narrow band, so a class C stage with a tuned tank gives the best efficiency without losing information.

questions.questionText: A power amplifier must amplify an amplitude-modulated signal whose envelope carries the information, without distorting that envelope. Which choice is suitable?
options: A class C stage with a tuned tank
A class C stage biased further below cut-off
questions.explanation: The output of a class C stage does not follow the input amplitude linearly, so it distorts the envelope; a linear class (A or AB) must be used to amplify an already-modulated signal.

questions.questionText: A transmitter must convert a 30 MHz oscillator signal into a 90 MHz signal efficiently. The usual choice is:
options: A class B push-pull stage with its tank tuned to 30 MHz
A class C stage with its tank tuned to 90 MHz
questions.explanation: The narrow class C current pulses are rich in harmonics; tuning the tank to the third harmonic selects 90 MHz (a frequency multiplier).

questions.questionText: The best class for the output stage of a battery-powered portable Bluetooth speaker, where battery life and small size matter most, is:
options: Class B with a large heat sink
questions.explanation: Class D switching stages exceed 90 % efficiency, giving the longest battery life and needing little or no heat sink.

questions.questionText: A microphone preamplifier handles signals of a few millivolts and delivers well under a milliwatt. Its amplifying stage is normally operated in:
questions.explanation: At such small power levels efficiency does not matter, and class A, which never switches off, gives the most faithful small-signal amplification.

questions.questionText: Class A operation is still used in small-signal stages despite its low efficiency because:
options: Class A has the highest efficiency at low signal levels
Class A needs no DC bias
The power involved is tiny, so the wasted power is negligible while the linearity is the best of all classes
questions.explanation: At milliwatt levels a few milliwatts of heat are unimportant, so linearity decides the choice. Class A efficiency is actually lowest at small signals.

questions.questionText: Which statement about amplifier classes is NOT correct?
options: A class A output transistor runs cooler at full output than with no signal
A class C stage can amplify audio if a large coupling capacitor is used
The transistors of a class D stage dissipate little because they are either fully on or fully off
A class B stage needs two transistors to reproduce the whole cycle
questions.explanation: Class C needs a tuned load and cannot reproduce a wideband audio signal whatever the coupling. The other three statements are correct.

questions.questionText: Compared with a class AB stage, a disadvantage of a class D audio amplifier is:
options: It needs an LC output filter and its fast switching edges can cause electromagnetic interference
It has a much lower efficiency
It needs a much larger heat sink
It cannot be made with MOSFETs
questions.explanation: Class D switches at a high frequency; an output filter must remove the switching component and careful layout is needed to limit EMI. Its efficiency and heat-sink needs are better than class AB.

questions.questionText: The switching frequency of a class D audio amplifier is chosen to be:
options: Well above the audio band, typically a few hundred kilohertz
Equal to the highest audio frequency, 20 kHz
Below 20 Hz so that it is inaudible
questions.explanation: The carrier must be far above 20 kHz so that the LC low-pass filter can remove it while passing the whole audio band; typical values are 250 kHz to 1 MHz.

questions.questionText: The output stage of an integrated-circuit op-amp is normally biased in class AB because:
options: It gives the highest possible efficiency of any class
It needs a tuned load that is easy to integrate
It allows the output transistors to operate as switches
It combines a small idle current with freedom from crossover distortion
questions.explanation: Class A would waste too much standby power and pure class B would add crossover distortion; class AB keeps the quiescent current small while both devices conduct near zero output.

questions.questionText: As the conduction angle of a class C stage is reduced from 180° towards very small values (same peak collector current), which is true?
options: Efficiency and output power both rise
Efficiency falls but output power rises
Efficiency rises towards 100 % but the output power falls
Efficiency stays at 78.5 % and output power is unchanged
questions.explanation: Shorter pulses flow only near the minimum collector voltage, so less is dissipated, but they contain less fundamental power; practical stages use about 120° to 150°.

questions.questionText: An oscilloscope shows the output sine wave of a power amplifier flattened at both positive and negative peaks, while the zero-crossing region is clean. The most likely cause is:
options: Crossover distortion of an unbiased class B stage
The input is driving the stage into saturation and cut-off (clipping)
Cancellation of even harmonics in the push-pull stage
questions.explanation: Flat tops at the peaks mean the output has reached the supply limits; crossover distortion would appear as a step near zero, not at the peaks.

questions.questionText: Crossover distortion in a class B stage is more objectionable at low volume than at high volume because:
options: The dead band of about 1.4 V is fixed, so it forms a larger fraction of a small signal
The transistors' gain falls at high volume
Crossover distortion only occurs when the output is below 1 W
The load impedance rises at low volume
questions.explanation: The step at the zero crossing is set by the two base-emitter drops, so its relative size, and therefore the percentage distortion, grows as the signal becomes smaller.

questions.questionText: For the same rated output power, which class needs the largest heat sink?
questions.explanation: A class A stage must dissipate its full quiescent power, twice the maximum output, continuously; the other classes dissipate far less.

questions.questionText: The maximum efficiency of a class AB push-pull stage lies:
options: Between the class A and class B values, roughly 50 % to 78.5 %
questions.explanation: The small quiescent current adds to the supply power, so class AB is slightly less efficient than ideal class B but far better than class A.

questions.questionText: Which class can reproduce the whole input cycle using only a single transistor?
questions.explanation: Only class A conducts for the full 360°. Classes B and AB need a push-pull pair, and class C conducts for less than half a cycle.

questions.questionText: Which loss mechanism in a class D stage increases in proportion to the switching frequency?
options: Switching loss during the on-off transitions of the transistors
Conduction loss in the on-resistance R_DS(on)
Power delivered to the load resistance
Quiescent bias loss of the output pair
questions.explanation: Each transition briefly has both voltage across and current through the switch, so the energy lost per transition is multiplied by the number of transitions per second. Conduction loss depends on I_rms² R_DS(on), not on frequency.

questions.questionText: Using the ideal efficiency relation η = (θ − sin θ)/(4[sin(θ/2) − (θ/2)cos(θ/2)]), a class C stage with a conduction angle of 120° has a maximum efficiency of about:
A 6 W output is needed. Ideally, the supply power required by a series-fed (resistive-load) class A stage and by a class B push-pull stage, both at their maximum efficiency, is:
options: 24 W for class A and 7.64 W for class B
12 W for class A and 7.64 W for class B
24 W for class A and 4.71 W for class B
6 W for class A and 7.64 W for class B
questions.explanation: Series-fed class A: 6/0.25 = 24 W; class B: 6/0.785 = 7.64 W. 12 W would apply to a transformer-coupled class A stage.

questions.questionText: Which statement correctly describes the trend from class A through class B to class C?
options: Conduction angle rises while efficiency falls
Efficiency rises while the conduction angle and linearity fall
questions.explanation: Class A conducts 360° with the best linearity and lowest efficiency; class C conducts least, is least linear and most efficient.

subtopics.title: Biasing Class AB Output Stage
subtopics.subtitle: A small quiescent bias removes the ±0.7 V dead zone at little cost in efficiency

concepts.text: From the Class B Dead Zone to Class AB

A complementary-symmetry class B stage places an npn transistor above a pnp transistor with their bases tied to the input and their emitters joined to the load. The npn device conducts only when the input exceeds about +0.7 V and the pnp only when it falls below about −0.7 V, so for inputs between those limits neither is on and the output stays at zero. This dead zone of roughly ±0.7 V (1.4 V wide) flattens the output at every zero crossing and is the origin of crossover distortion. Because the notch is a fixed 1.4 V, quiet passages suffer proportionally far more than loud ones, and the distortion consists of harsh odd harmonics.

Class AB removes the dead zone by holding the two bases about 2V_BE (1.2 V to 1.4 V) apart with a bias network, so that both transistors carry a small quiescent current I_Q with no signal. Each device now conducts for slightly more than 180°, both are on near the zero crossing, and the transfer characteristic becomes a smooth straight line. Typical I_Q is a few milliamperes in small stages and 20 mA to 100 mA in loudspeaker amplifiers, small compared with peak load currents of several amperes. The stage remains a push-pull emitter follower: voltage gain near unity, large current gain and low output impedance.
Biasing Methods

Resistor divider. The simplest network is a resistive divider from the positive to the negative supply with a small resistor between the two bases; the current through the chain drops about 1.4 V across that resistor. It is cheap and needs no matched parts, but the bias voltage is fixed while the transistors' V_BE falls by about 2 mV per °C as they warm up, so the quiescent current rises with temperature, producing more heat and a further rise. This method is therefore used only together with emitter resistors and at modest power levels.

Diode bias. Two diodes in series between the bases, fed by a constant current from resistors or current sources, provide a bias voltage of two diode drops that closely matches the two V_BE values of the output pair. If the diodes are mounted on the same heat sink as the output transistors, their forward voltage falls with temperature at nearly the same rate as V_BE, so the bias tracks the transistors and I_Q stays almost constant: this is thermal compensation. The quiescent current is set by the diode current and by the ratio of transistor to diode junction areas. Diode bias is compact and is the standard method inside integrated circuits and op-amp output stages, but the bias voltage cannot be trimmed.

V_BE multiplier. A small transistor with resistor R1 from collector to base and R2 from base to emitter is connected between the two output bases. The transistor adjusts its collector current until the voltage across R2 equals its own V_BE, so the divider forces the total voltage across the network to V_BE(1 + R1/R2). It behaves as an amplified diode whose voltage can be set to any multiple of V_BE, usually with a trimmer in R1 or R2 to adjust I_Q precisely, and it tracks temperature when its transistor is mounted on the heat sink. It is the preferred bias element in discrete high-quality audio amplifiers.

concepts.plainText: V_bias = V_BE (1 + R1/R2)

concepts.text: Quiescent Current, Efficiency and Thermal Runaway

Choosing I_Q is a trade-off. A larger I_Q gives a smoother hand-over and lower distortion at small signals, but the standby power 2V_CC I_Q (for ±V_CC supplies) is dissipated as heat even in silence, pulling the efficiency below the 78.5 % class B ideal towards class A values. Thermal runaway is the danger: at a fixed base voltage the collector current increases steeply as the junction warms, more current means more heat, and without correction the transistor destroys itself. Three measures prevent it:
Protection against thermal runaway:
items: Thermally coupled bias elements: the bias diodes or the V_BE-multiplier transistor are mounted on the output heat sink so the bias voltage falls (about 2 mV per °C per junction) as the output devices warm.

Emitter resistors R_E of 0.1 Ω to 1 Ω in series with each emitter: any rise in I_Q increases the drop across R_E and reduces the effective V_BE, which is negative feedback that limits the current; they also equalise current sharing between imperfectly matched transistors.
A heat sink large enough to keep the junction temperature well below its limit at the worst-case dissipation.

concepts.text: The Complementary-Symmetry Stage

The complementary-symmetry output stage uses an npn and a pnp transistor as a pair of emitter followers and needs neither an output transformer nor a phase splitter: the same input drives both bases and each conducts on the appropriate half-cycle. With a single supply the output rests at V_CC/2 and reaches the loudspeaker through a large coupling capacitor; with dual supplies the output rests at 0 V and the load is connected directly. The bias network sits between the two bases and is driven by a class A voltage-amplifier (driver) stage. Where matched pnp power transistors are unavailable, a quasi-complementary design uses two npn power devices driven by a complementary pair of smaller transistors.

None; I_Q drifts upward as the devices warm

Adjustable with a trimmer; used in discrete hi-fi amplifiers

concepts.text: Worked Example: Setting the Quiescent Current

A complementary stage runs from ±20 V with two bias diodes of 0.70 V each between the bases, so V_bias = 1.40 V. At the quiescent point each output transistor needs V_BE = 0.65 V, leaving 1.40 − 1.30 = 0.10 V across the two 0.5 Ω emitter resistors, so I_Q = 0.10 V / 1.0 Ω = 100 mA and the standby dissipation is 2 × 20 V × 0.1 A = 4 W (2 W per transistor) before any signal is applied. Reducing I_Q to 20 mA, by running the diodes at a lower current or using slightly larger emitter resistors, cuts the standby loss to 0.8 W while still eliminating the dead zone. If the diodes are fed at 5 mA, the two feed resistors must drop 40 − 1.4 = 38.6 V between them, so each is about 38.6 V / (2 × 5 mA), roughly 3.9 kΩ.
Going Deeper: Setting and Holding the Quiescent Current

The V_BE multiplier result follows from two facts. The multiplier transistor adjusts its own collector current until the voltage across R2 (base to emitter) equals its V_BE, so the current in R2 is V_BE/R2. If the base current is small, the same current flows through R1, so the total voltage is V_BE/R2 × (R1 + R2) = V_BE(1 + R1/R2). Whatever part of the incoming bias current is not needed by the resistor chain simply flows through the transistor. Because the whole voltage is a multiple of one V_BE, its temperature coefficient is multiplied by the same factor: a network set to 2V_BE falls by about 4 mV/°C, exactly matching the two output junctions it must track.

concepts.plainText: dV_bias/dT = (1 + R1/R2) × dV_BE/dT  (≈ −2 mV/°C per V_BE)

concepts.text: Why is fixed bias so dangerous? Collector current depends exponentially on V_BE, I_C = I_S e^(V_BE/V_T), so an extra 18 mV of base-emitter voltage doubles the current and about 60 mV multiplies it by ten (V_T = 26 mV). At a fixed bias voltage, a temperature rise of only 9 °C lowers the required V_BE by 18 mV, which is the same as applying 18 mV more drive, and the current doubles. Emitter resistors change the law: the quiescent current becomes (V_bias − 2V_BE)/(2R_E), which responds only linearly and gently to a change in V_BE, and good thermal tracking of V_bias removes most of the remaining drift.

concepts.plainText: I_C2/I_C1 = e^(ΔV_BE/V_T); doubling needs ΔV_BE = V_T ln 2 ≈ 18 mV (V_T = 26 mV)

concepts.text: Emitter resistors are a compromise. Larger R_E stabilises I_Q better and forces paralleled transistors to share current, but every ampere of load current drops I × R_E across them, which wastes power and reduces the available output swing, so values of 0.1 Ω to 0.5 Ω are usual. With Darlington or compound output devices the bias network must supply four junction drops instead of two, about 2.6 V, which is easy with a multiplier and needs four diodes otherwise. In integrated circuits the bias diodes are diode-connected transistors that form current mirrors with the output devices, so I_Q equals the bias current multiplied by the ratio of emitter areas.
Common mistakes in class AB bias calculations:
items: Writing V_bias = V_BE × R1/R2 and forgetting the 1 in (1 + R1/R2).
Using one R_E instead of 2R_E: the quiescent current flows through both emitter resistors in series between the two emitters.
Counting the standby power from one rail only; with ±V_CC supplies it is 2V_CC I_Q.
Treating the bias diodes as if they carried the load current; they carry only the bias current, which must exceed the peak base current of the output transistors.
Mounting the bias element on the circuit board; without thermal coupling there is no tracking.

concepts.text: When adjusting a trimmer in a V_BE multiplier, start from the low-bias end and increase slowly while watching I_Q. Arrange the trimmer so that a worn or open wiper lowers the bias rather than raising it, because an open R1 drives the quiescent current to destructive levels.

Two numbers carry most bias questions: −2 mV/°C for every junction and 18 mV (at V_T = 26 mV) to double the current. Together they show that a 9 °C rise with untracked, undegenerated bias doubles I_Q.

notes.text: Diode bias works because a diode's forward drop matches a transistor's V_BE (about 0.7 V) and falls with temperature at the same rate (about −2 mV/°C). Both halves of that sentence are exam answers: matching and thermal compensation.

Bias diodes or the V_BE-multiplier transistor must be thermally coupled to the output transistors (mounted on the same heat sink). Electrically correct bias with no thermal coupling still allows thermal runaway.
Increasing the quiescent current lowers crossover distortion but raises standby dissipation and lowers efficiency; class AB is a compromise, and at very large I_Q it turns into class A.
V_BE multiplier: V_bias = V_BE(1 + R1/R2). With R1 = R2 it produces 2V_BE and replaces the two diodes; it is also called an amplified diode.

formulas.title: Class AB bias voltage
formulas.description: Voltage held between the two bases of a complementary pair so that both transistors are just conducting at zero signal.

formulas.title: V_BE multiplier
formulas.description: R1 from collector to base and R2 from base to emitter of the bias transistor; the network acts as an adjustable, temperature-tracking diode.

formulas.title: Quiescent current with emitter resistors
formulas.description: V_BE(Q) is each output transistor's base-emitter voltage at the quiescent point and R_E is each emitter resistor; use it to set or check I_Q.

formulas.title: Standby dissipation
formulas.description: Heat produced with no signal by a class AB pair running from ±V_CC supplies (V_CC I_Q with a single supply), shared equally by the two transistors.

flashcards.front: How wide is the dead zone of an unbiased complementary class B stage, and what causes it?
flashcards.back: About 1.4 V (±0.7 V): each base-emitter junction needs about 0.7 V before it conducts, so near zero input neither transistor is on.

flashcards.front: Why are the bias diodes of a class AB stage mounted on the output transistors' heat sink?
flashcards.back: So that their forward voltage falls with temperature at the same rate as the transistors' V_BE, keeping the quiescent current constant and preventing thermal runaway.

flashcards.front: State two ways emitter resistors help a class AB output stage.
flashcards.back: They stabilise I_Q against temperature (a rise in current increases the drop across R_E and reduces the effective V_BE) and they equalise current sharing between the two transistors.

questions.questionText: In a diode-biased class AB output stage the two bias diodes are mounted on the same heat sink as the output transistors so that:
options: Their forward voltage tracks the transistors' V_BE with temperature, holding the quiescent current steady
They can carry the full load current
The stage can operate without any emitter resistors
questions.explanation: A diode drop and a transistor V_BE both fall by about 2 mV per °C. Thermally coupling them makes the bias voltage fall as the transistors warm, which prevents the quiescent current from rising (thermal runaway).

questions.questionText: A V_BE multiplier uses R1 = 1 kΩ (collector to base) and R2 = 1 kΩ (base to emitter). If its transistor's V_BE is 0.65 V, the bias voltage across the network is:
questions.explanation: V_bias = V_BE(1 + R1/R2) = 0.65 × (1 + 1) = 1.30 V, which is the 2V_BE needed to bias a complementary pair into class AB.

questions.questionText: Small resistors of 0.1 Ω to 1 Ω are connected in series with the emitters of a class AB complementary pair mainly to:
options: Increase the voltage gain of the stage
Stabilise the quiescent current against thermal runaway and equalise current sharing
Provide the 1.4 V bias between the bases
Match the loudspeaker impedance to the transistors
questions.explanation: If I_Q rises, the extra drop across R_E reduces the effective base-emitter voltage and limits the current (negative feedback); the resistors also share current evenly between imperfectly matched devices.

questions.questionText: An unbiased complementary emitter-follower (class B) stage with silicon transistors (V_BE = 0.7 V) is driven by a 2 V peak sine wave. The peak output voltage is about:
questions.explanation: Each transistor conducts only after its base-emitter drop is overcome, so the output peak is 2.0 − 0.7 = 1.3 V. Subtracting the full 1.4 V dead band (0.6 V) is the usual slip.

questions.questionText: A complementary emitter-follower stage with silicon transistors, correctly biased into class AB, is driven by a 2 V peak sine wave into its load. The peak output voltage is about:
options: 1.3 V, because V_BE is still lost on each half-cycle
2 V, because the biased emitter followers have a gain close to 1 and no dead zone
0.6 V, because both transistors conduct at once
4 V, because the bias adds voltage gain
questions.explanation: The bias network supplies the base-emitter drops, so the output follows the input with the gain of an emitter follower, slightly less than 1.

questions.questionText: An unbiased complementary class B stage (V_BE = 0.7 V for each transistor) is driven by a 1 V peak sine wave. For roughly what fraction of each cycle is neither transistor conducting?
questions.explanation: Neither conducts while |sin ωt| < 0.7, i.e. within 44.4° of each zero crossing. That is 4 × 44.4° = 177.7° of 360°, about 49 % of the cycle.

questions.questionText: With no emitter resistors, the voltage needed between the bases of a complementary silicon output pair to bring both transistors just into conduction is about:
questions.explanation: Each base-emitter junction needs about 0.7 V, and the two junctions are in series between the bases, so about 2V_BE = 1.4 V is required.

questions.questionText: At constant current, the forward voltage of a silicon diode changes with temperature by approximately:
questions.explanation: Both a diode's forward drop and a transistor's V_BE fall by about 2 mV for every °C rise, which is why diodes can track the output transistors.

questions.questionText: A class AB stage uses a Darlington pair on each side of the output (four base-emitter junctions between the two input bases). If simple diode bias is used, the number of diodes required is:
questions.explanation: One diode is needed for each base-emitter junction in the path between the two driving bases: 2 per Darlington, 4 in total, about 2.6 V to 2.8 V.

questions.questionText: The bias transistor of a V_BE multiplier has V_BE = 0.6 V, with 2.2 kΩ between its collector and base and 1 kΩ between its base and emitter. The multiplier holds the two output bases apart by:
questions.explanation: V_bias = V_BE(1 + R1/R2) = 0.6 × (1 + 2.2) = 1.92 V. Forgetting the 1 gives 1.32 V; inverting the ratio gives 0.87 V.

questions.questionText: A V_BE multiplier must produce 1.8 V using a transistor with V_BE = 0.6 V and R2 = 1.2 kΩ (base to emitter). The required R1 (collector to base) is:
questions.explanation: 1 + R1/R2 = 1.8/0.6 = 3, so R1/R2 = 2 and R1 = 2 × 1.2 = 2.4 kΩ. Taking R1/R2 = 3 gives the wrong 3.6 kΩ.

questions.questionText: A V_BE multiplier uses R1 = 2 kΩ and R2 = 1 kΩ, and its transistor's V_BE changes by −2 mV/°C. The temperature coefficient of the bias voltage is:
questions.explanation: The whole voltage is V_BE(1 + R1/R2) = 3V_BE, so its coefficient is 3 × (−2) = −6 mV/°C.

questions.questionText: A class AB pair with 0.47 Ω emitter resistors must idle at I_Q = 50 mA with V_BE(Q) = 0.6 V for each output transistor. The bias comes from a V_BE multiplier with V_BE = 0.6 V and R2 = 1 kΩ. The required R1 is about:
questions.explanation: V_bias = 2(0.6) + 2(0.05)(0.47) = 1.247 V; R1/R2 = 1.247/0.6 − 1 = 1.078, so R1 = 1.08 kΩ. Ignoring the emitter-resistor drop gives 1.00 kΩ.

questions.questionText: A class AB stage has V_bias = 1.4 V between the bases, V_BE(Q) = 0.62 V for each output transistor and 0.47 Ω emitter resistors. The quiescent current is about:
questions.explanation: I_Q = (V_bias − 2V_BE(Q))/(2R_E) = (1.4 − 1.24)/(0.94) = 0.170 A. Using a single R_E gives 340 mA.

questions.questionText: A class AB stage has fixed resistor-divider bias V_bias = 1.4 V (no thermal tracking), R_E = 0.5 Ω in each emitter and V_BE(Q) = 0.65 V at 25 °C. If the output transistors warm by 20 °C and each V_BE(Q) falls at 2 mV/°C, the quiescent current changes from 100 mA to about:
questions.explanation: New V_BE(Q) = 0.65 − 0.04 = 0.61 V; I_Q = (1.4 − 1.22)/(2 × 0.5) = 0.18 A. Changing only one transistor's V_BE gives 140 mA.

questions.questionText: An output transistor with no emitter resistor is held at a fixed base-emitter voltage while it warms by 25 °C. Taking dV_BE/dT = −2 mV/°C and V_T = 26 mV, its collector current increases by a factor of about:
questions.explanation: The 50 mV reduction in the required V_BE acts like 50 mV extra drive: I_C2/I_C1 = e^(50/26) = e^1.92 = 6.8. The linear ratio 50/26 = 1.9 is a common slip.

questions.questionText: Taking V_T = 26 mV, by how much must a transistor's base-emitter voltage increase to double its collector current?
questions.explanation: I_C ∝ e^(V_BE/V_T), so doubling needs ΔV_BE = V_T ln 2 = 26 × 0.693 = 18 mV. About 60 mV gives a tenfold increase.

questions.questionText: A class AB stage running from ±25 V supplies has a quiescent current of 40 mA. Its total standby dissipation is:
questions.explanation: P_standby = 2V_CC I_Q = 2 × 25 × 0.04 = 2 W, shared equally (1 W per transistor). Using one rail only gives 1 W.

questions.questionText: A complementary stage on ±20 V drives an 8 Ω load with a full 20 V peak swing (ideal). Pure class B would then have 78.5 % efficiency. If it is biased into class AB with I_Q = 100 mA and the supply is assumed to draw the class B current plus I_Q, the efficiency becomes about:
questions.explanation: P_L = 20²/(2 × 8) = 25 W; class B P_dc = 2 × 20 × 2.5/π = 31.8 W; standby adds 2 × 20 × 0.1 = 4 W; η = 25/35.8 = 69.8 %. Counting only one rail's 2 W gives 73.9 %.

questions.questionText: Two bias diodes (0.7 V each) and two 2.2 kΩ resistors are connected in series from +15 V to −15 V, with the diodes between the output bases. Neglecting base currents, the diode current is about:
questions.explanation: I = (30 − 1.4)/(2 × 2.2 kΩ) = 28.6/4.4 kΩ = 6.5 mA. Taking only half the 28.6 V drop gives about 3.3 mA; using one resistor gives 13 mA.

questions.questionText: In a diode-biased class AB stage the peak load current is 2 A and the output transistors have β = 50. The current supplied to the bias chain must be at least about:
questions.explanation: At the signal peak the conducting output transistor needs I_B = 2/50 = 40 mA from the bias chain; if the chain current were smaller, the peak would be clipped.

questions.questionText: In an IC output stage the bias diodes are diode-connected transistors matched to the output transistors, which have four times their emitter area. With 2 mA through the diodes and no emitter resistors, the quiescent current is:
questions.explanation: Matched junctions at the same V_BE form a current mirror; current scales with emitter area, so I_Q = 4 × 2 mA = 8 mA.

questions.questionText: A single-supply complementary class AB stage runs from V_CC = 24 V, with the loudspeaker connected through a coupling capacitor. With no signal, the DC voltage at the joined emitters should be:
questions.explanation: With one supply the output node rests at V_CC/2 = 12 V so that it can swing equally up and down; the coupling capacitor blocks this DC from the load.

questions.questionText: A class AB emitter-follower output stage has R_E = 0.5 Ω in series with each emitter and drives an 8 Ω load. Neglecting the transistors' internal emitter resistance, its voltage gain is about:
questions.explanation: The conducting half is a follower whose output divides between R_E and R_L: A_v = R_L/(R_L + R_E) = 8/8.5 = 0.941.

questions.questionText: A class AB stage delivers a sine wave of 3 A peak to its load; each emitter resistor is 0.33 Ω and carries the current of its own half-cycle only. Neglecting I_Q, the average power dissipated in EACH emitter resistor is about:
questions.explanation: A half-wave sine current of peak I_p has mean-square value I_p²/4, so P = 9 × 0.33/4 = 0.74 W. Assuming a full sine wave (I_p²/2) gives 1.49 W.

questions.questionText: A class AB stage delivers 3 A peak to its load and has R_E = 0.33 Ω in each emitter. The peak voltage lost across the conducting emitter resistor, which reduces the available output swing, is about:
questions.explanation: V = I_p × R_E = 3 × 0.33 = 0.99 V; only one emitter resistor carries the load current at a time.

questions.questionText: A class AB pair is biased by two diodes giving V_bias = 1.3 V, and each output transistor has V_BE(Q) = 0.6 V. To obtain I_Q = 50 mA, each emitter resistor must be:
